22000: Observation Point at the northwest end of Normanby Island (Milne Bay Province) is the home of a taxocene with four to five species of sand divers, Trichonotus, one of them the recently described T. halstead. In 1997 and 1998 we returned to study their early life history. Purported gill-chamber brooding was not confirmed by dissections of many specimens. The sympatric species live in distinct harem territories or swarms on a sandy slope where they mate soon after sunrise. T. setiger, mating over coarse sand, deposit many small eggs. Mature females (~ 8.7 cm TL) had ovaries with 150 to 200 oocytes. When mating is over, eggs were scooped up with sand from the mating site, rushed into the boat, and observed live under special microscopes. Deposited translucent eggs (0.6 mm) stick to the sand grains. The clear yolk contains one large yellowish oil globule. Development was observed at 25-26 C: after 30 min, four cells had formed. Ten hours later, heart beat and blood circulation could be seen. Hatching occurred 13-13.5 hours after spawning. The just hatched embryos (ca. 2.2 mm TL, >38 somites) were translucent with completely unpigmented eyes. Initially the embryos were mostly resting at the bottom, occasionally wriggling, later darting around and into the water column. When motionless, they slowly sank head first. At 18 h a white pigment was observed around the anus, later white pigment accumulated around the notochord towards the tip of the tail, and finally in the head region. When one day old (3 mm TL) the yolksac had decreased in size; initially, the oil globule was about 1/4 of the yolksac length, now it took 1/3 of yolk size. At age two days the embryos had reached a TL of 4.5 mm. The snout region had become more pointed but neither jaw movements nor gut contents were observed, i.e. exogenous feeding was not yet started. These findings will be discussed with respect to the distribution of the sand divers and a possible direct development without a planktonic larva, a rare thing in coral reef fishes.

22001: Food habits data collected on Northeast Fisheries Science Center groundfish surveys between Nova Scotia and Cape Fear from 1981-1990 were analyzed to categorize abundant species into feeding types (e.g., piscivorus, molluscivorus, etc.), and to examine changes in feeding types through ontogeny. Over 83,000 stomach samples from 51 species (13 elasmobranch, 36 teleost, and 2 cephalopod species) were included in the analysis. Predator feeding types representing primary reliance on Annelida (Glyptocephalus cynoglossus, Pleuronectes americanus and Pleuronectes ferrugineus), Arthropoda (9 species including 4 > 80%: Sebastes fasciatus, Scomber scombrus, Raja senta, and Mustelus canis), Mollusca (Myliobatis freminvillei and Merluccius albidus), Echinodermata (Hippoglossoides platessoides), and Fish (17 species including 4 > 90%: Pomatomus saltatrix, Carcharhinus plumbeus, Synodus foetens, and Lophius americanus) were found. Other prey groups were relatively unimportant. The remaining 18 species did not rely primarily on any one group. We also describe feeding types based on the observed patterns of change among 5-10 cm predator size classes. For example, a primary piscivore (e.g. Lophius americanus) relies predominately on fish throughout its sampled size range, while a positive secondary piscivore increases (e.g., Merluccius bilinearis, Gadus morhua), and a negative secondary piscivore decreases (Pomatomus saltatrix), its reliance on fish as it grows.

22002: Discussions of the influence of riparian vegetation on stream health focus on the width of such buffer zones. Policy decisions and environmental regulations similarly use riparian width as the metric of importance. We sampled fishes and stream habitats in 12 stream segments downstream from deforested riparian patches 0 - 5.6 km long, all downslope from densely forested watersheds. We found that the strongest predictors of fish abundance and occurrence were area and particularly length of the riparian patch; patch width was a relatively poor predictor of fish occurrence. Limited riparian clearing may cause minor disturbance to the fish assemblage, but streams in even a heavily forested watershed cannot tolerate disruption of the riparian zone of much more than 1 km in length. Riparian buffer length should be given stronger consideration in stream protection and restoration plans.

22003: The Spiny dogfish is the most abundant shark in B.C. waters with biomass estimated to be approximately 200,000 t. Frequenting all depths within coastal shelf and slope habitats, the dogfish is a significant predator within NE Pacific ecosystems impacting a wide variety of vertebrate and invertebrate taxonomic groups spanning several trophic levels. In this paper we summarize the feeding habits of the spiny dogfish in B.C. waters analyzing several data sets collected during the 1970's and 1980's, and comparing them to published literature. In particular, we examine the spatial and temporal variability in dogfish feeding habits and discuss the importance of recognizing bias when attempting to estimate consumption rates of dogfish prey.
22004: Measuring food consumption in elasmobranch fishes has proven to be a challenge, and has resulted in the use of a variety of methods. In recent years, bioenergetics models have increased in popularity and complexity. These models take into account energetic costs of living (metabolism, wastes, and growth) in order to estimate consumption requirements. Bioenergetics models have been used to estimate consumption rates for a number of different species including lemon, sandbar, greyreef, galapagos, tiger, bull, spiny dogfish, scalloped hammerhead sharks, and spiny butterfly ray. Like all models, output is reliant on the quality of input data, thus direct measurements of the costs of living and how costs vary with environmental variables and body size are needed. A complete model has been assembled for the lemon shark, which through laboratory and field research has shown good cross-validation. However, accuracy of some models may be questionable due to inclusion of data from other species or by using laboratory data alone. Recent advances in telemetry techniques and captive husbandry may offer new opportunities for estimating energetic parameters in both the field and laboratory. Bioenergetics models may also be useful in quantifying the ecological association of elasmobranchs on habitats and prey populations.
22005: Much of the communication behavior of anuran amphibians and other vertebrates takes place in the context of reproduction. Many aspects of communication are dependent on, influenced by, hormones associated with reproductive state. Less clearly appreciated is the fact that communication signals influence hormonal state in a variety of vertebrates. Communication and endocrine state should therefore be considered mutually interacting systems. We have used anuran amphibians as a model for investigating this interaction. Our results indicate that the frog auditory system (carrying information about vocal communication signals) connects with several areas of the basal forebrain. Some of these areas contain gonadotropin releasing hormone cells while others contain populations of catecholamine neurons. The latter populations are sensitive to circulating sex steroid hormones, and may be involved in some aspect of reproductive endocrinology or behavior. The strong connections between auditory and endocrine systems in frogs suggest that the reception of communication signals may influence gonadal state. Experiments exposing frogs to conspecific calls support this. Males exposed to conspecific calls showed larger testes and changes in testes histology compared to control animals. In frogs, therefore, vocal communication signals trigger changes in reproductive physiology as well as reproductive behavior.
22006: Male anurans of many species advertise for mates vocally in dense aggregations where they may also interact aggressively with competitors. Recently, sophisticated experimental techniques have been used to address questions about the proximate and ultimate bases of vocal behavior of these animals. For example, with interactive playback an analog or computer-based call synthesizer is made to respond to a calling male after user-specified time delays. I will discuss how I have used this methodology in work on call timing and aggressive behavior. Our understanding of the calling dynamics of chorus members has also benefited from the use of multi-channel equipment to monitor the vocal behavior of two or more males. By using such a system in my studies of Hyla microcephala in Panama, I have found that males respond primarily to their nearest neighbors in the chorus. These results agree with recent findings on acoustically signaling insects. The behavior of males minimizes signal overlap with individuals whose calls are most likely to seriously impair their ability to attract a female. I will also discuss data on vocal interactions among male H. versicolor obtained in an artificial pond where my colleagues and I have manipulated chorus density.

22007: Xenopus laevis is a nocturnal Pipid whose native habitat is the murky ponds of South Africa. Two vocal behaviors had been characterized: the advertisement call of sexually receptive males and the release call (ticking) of sexually unreceptive females. We have recently described an additional vocal signal, a fertility advertisement called rapping, given by females just prior to oviposition. Rapping is an acoustic aphrodisiac that stimulates male calling and phonotaxis. Field and laboratory observations suggest that calling is confined to only one or two males at any one time, even in densely populated ponds. We have recorded several male/male vocalizations (e.g. chirping and growling) that might serve to establish male vocal hierarchies at the onset of the breeding season. I will discuss the significance of these calls in reproductive interactions and the cellular and molecular mechanisms that contribute to the sexually differentiated vocal repertoire.
22008: Midwife toads are a primitive group of anurans with parental care and highly simplified vocal communication. Several populations of Alytes have been studied in continental Spain since 1987. The distributions of call characteristics overlapped between different population and species. The covariance between temperature and call duration varied between populations of different taxonomic groups. Large male reproductive advantage was found. Phonotaxis tests showed that calls with lower frequencies (emitted by larger males) were more attractive to females than calls with high frequencies. In syntopic populations of the two species there was no sign of character displacement in the male calls, but female preference was different than in allopatric situations. Males increase their calling rate when exposed to a nearby competitor. The response is different according to competitor's size and competitor's calling rate. Call alternation between males is non-random. Although call overlap affects negatively female preference, call alternation does not decrease call overlap. Many of the differences observed in acoustical competition can be related with the differences in mating season length between species, and with the differences in selective pressures that these two scenarios incorporate (male acoustical competition, and female choice based in both dynamic and static call characteristics).

22009: The asian green toads have been profitably employed as a model for the study of the evolution of vocalizations by comparing diploid, triploid and tetraploid green toads on the basis of morphometrical and acoustical parameters. Since in green toads advertisement calls produced by males play an important role in mate choice, particular attention is given to their differences. Diploid toads show significantly larger body size and proportionally larger head and shorter limbs than both tetraploids and triploids, whereas no evident morphometrical differences were observed between triploids and tetraploids. Diploid advertisement calls have spectral and temporal properties that significantly differ from those of both triploid and tetraploid advertisement calls. Diploids produce significantly longer calls with higher pulse-rates and lower frequencies than those of tetraploids. Although strong associations are found between some temporal and spectral call parameters and body size of the calling male, our analyses demonstrate that the observed differences in advertisement calls cannot be explained as the by-product of body size differentiation only. We address the question of the factors that could be responsible for these differences: whether they are a direct consequence of poliploidy or, whether they should be seen as the result of an evolutionary process of diversification.

22010: The diversity of sizes and shapes within and among groups of fishes is one of the principal features of their evolutionary history. To understand as much as possible about the history of size and shape evolution, two important components must be explored: phylogeny and environment. The evolution of size and shape have often been discussed in the context of developmental theories involving differential growth (allometry), differential timing (heterochrony), developmental integration, etc. The purpose of this presentation will be to examine ways in which developmental theories of size and shape diversity are tested on phylogenetic and environmental hypotheses. The data comprise ontogenetic series of landmarks from clades of characid (Bryconops) and atherinopsid (Atherinella) fishes, fit to a reference form, from which the relative warps and relative-warp scores are calculated. Phylogenetic and environmental components of form change among species within clades is analyzed from both partial least squares confirmatory factor analyses. The results show that in contrast to expectations derived from the literature, large amounts of the variance in form-change among species are explained by phylogenetic hypotheses of species relationships.

22011: Barbus paludinosus, a diploid, small African barb species is widely distributed from South Africa to the Horn of Africa. It was previously reported from the Ethiopian Rift Valley and the closely related species, B. humilis, was reported from Lake Tana. We found B. paludinosus in the upper reaches of the White Nile, Blue Nile, and Omo River drainages. This species normally has a strong serrated spine in the dorsal fin. At two localities in the upper reaches of the White Nile and Omo tributaries, populations are characterized by a greatly reduced dorsal spine. In the same drainages, barbs with the normal dorsal spine morphology occur about 20 km downstream. The borderline between forms with normal and reduced dorsal spine morphology apparently coincides with the upper limit of distribution of the hexaploid large barb species, the only potential predator in the naturally depauperated fish communities inhabiting the upper reaches of the both river drainages. The distance between locations where the form with reduced dorsal spine occurs is more than 200 km. These locations are separated by the drainage system of a large tributary of the Blue Nile, where only the normal form was found. The morphological description of the Ethiopian populations of B. paludinosus with and without dorsal spine is presented. In order to test hypothesis about independent reduction of the dorsal spine in barbs from the two distant locations the karyological and mtDNA comparisons were made.

22012: The upper Coosa River basin poses a particularly perplexing biogeographic problem; it harbors isolated populations of many species of fishes otherwise found below the Fall Line. Over 17 species exhibit this distributional pattern to some degree. The already recognized high degree of endemism in the drainage (Percina antesella, P. jenkinsi, Etheostoma etowahae, E. scotti, etc.) suggests the possibility of cryptic species in other, more 'widespread' taxa. We examined morphometric and meristic variation across the range of the frecklebelly madtom, Noturus munitus. The populations in the Etowah and Conasauga Rivers possess a unique suite of morphological characters, including differences in shape and pigmentation, when compared with populations from the Pearl, Cahaba, and Tombigbee Rivers. We are in the process of analyzing genetic variation within this species and other closely related members of Rabida to identify phylogenetic relationships within this complex. Conservation and biogeographic implications will be discussed.

22013: Patterns of morphological variation in a group of western North American cyprinid fishes (the 'Gila robusta' complex of the Gila River basin of Arizona and New Mexico) has long puzzled fish taxonomists. Three different forms, (G. robusta, G. intermedia, and G. nigra) are recognized, yet their basin-wide distributions are a disjunct mosaic. Several hypotheses have been offered to accommodate this aberrant pattern: ecotypy/ecophenotypy (i.e., individual or populational response to local conditions), hybridization/intergradation (i.e., gene flow between differentiated species or races); and vicariance (an historical explanation related to regional hydrographic evolution). To represent these hypotheses, 33 sample locations were scored within the basin with regard to stream size, stream elevation, stream barriers, and paleodrainage pattern (the latter accomplished by superimposing sites onto maps depicting drainage patterns during six different geologic epochs). Morphometric data, collected from 25 individuals at all 33 sites, were then contrasted against the 9 test matrices using two- and three-way Mantel tests. A vicariance model was the only hypothesis proficient in explaining extant diversity of fish phenotypes. Of those reconstructions used in this model, only the Pliocene epoch was significantly associated with extant distributions of phenotypes.

22014: Gynogenetic female Amazon mollies (Poecilia formosa) mate with sexual males (P. latipinna) for successful reproduction. Studies show that males distinguish between conspecific females and gynogens, and preferentially mate with the former. However, the existence of gynogens indicates mate discrimination is imperfect. The Red Queen Hypothesis has been applied to this system suggesting the evolution of mate recognition is a coevolutionary 'arms race'; the lack of genetic contribution by males to gynogenetic offspring imposes selection for male discrimination that favors sexual females. This, in turn, imposes selection on gynogens to evolve characters that override male discrimination. This assumes gynogenetic females have evolved since their origination. Amazons originated with a hybridization between P. mexicana and P. latipinna at least several thousand years ago. If a coevolutionary hypothesis is true, extant gynogens should differ from ancestral gynogens. In this study first generation sexual hybrids were used as an analog for the ancestral gynogens to test this hypothesis. The predictions are gynogens will have an enhanced ability to attract sexual males, males will prefer gynogens over hybrids, and females will differ in agonistic behavior. The results of this study do not support these predictions. This suggests application of such hypotheses to gynogenetic systems be preceded by studies documenting the presence of evolutionary change in the species of interest.

22015: The sandbasses of the genus Paralabrax are New World fishes from the Eastern Pacific and Western Atlantic. Because the sister group relationships of the Serranin genera related to Paralabrax were unknown, they were resolved first. Osteological characters of the cranium and pelvic girdle support the monophyly of Cratinus-Paralabrax-Centropristis. The nine species of Paralabrax share derived features of urohyal configuration, pterygiophore structure in dorsal and anal fins, and structure of lateral line scales. A cladistic analysis based on morphological and molecular (cytochrome b gene) data suggests an early separation of two groups. One is predominantly South American and includes 5 species: dewegeri from the Atlantic (Venezuela-Brazil), humeralis (Chile-Peru), callaensis (Ecuador), and albomaculatus (Galapagos). Interestingly, the species clathratus belongs to this group but is found in the Northeastern Pacific. The other group is composed of 4 Northern hemisphere species: loro (Central America-Baja California), auroguttatus, maculatofasciatus and nebulifer (which are predominantly found from Baja to Central California). A hypothesis of relationships is presented. The species of Paralabrax seem to have evolved recently, in the last 4-10 million years, in contrast with the species of Centropristis, which appear to be significantly older.

22016: Patterns of geographical variation in AP-PCR (RAPD) markers were compared between two species of Poeciliid fishes. Thirty-one populations of the variable platyfish Xiphophorus variatus and thirteen populations of the killifish Heterandria jonesi were studied. These species overlap in range in central-eastern Mexico, in freshwaters from the Rio Tamesi drainage, south to the Rio Nautla. Six primers revealed 266 scoreable bands in X. variatus and 189 in H. jonesi (163 and 124 informative characters, respectively). Parsimony analysis of the data was performed in X. variatus by heuristic search for the shortest cladograms. The data for H. jonesi are still being gathered, and a subset of only eight populations was analysed (exhaustive search). The results support three geographically disjunct clades in each species: a northern clade centered in the Tamesi drainage, a south-eastern clade in the lowlands of the Rios Cazones, Tecolutla, Solteros and Nautla, and a south-western clade, more upstream in these rivers. We hypothesize that the same geographical barriers have affected the variation in both species. Relevant geographic barriers are not obvious, however. We suggest that the south-eastern and south-western populations are divided by elevation, while the northern populations are separated from the southern populations by unsuitable habitat of slow-flowing waters. It is also worth noting that populations of X. evelynae are nested entirely within the geographic range of the south-west clade and are indistinguishable from them. This raises the question of whether it is a valid species or whether all of the fish in the south-west clade might really be X. evelynae, rather than X. variatus.

22017: The study aims at resolving the taxonomic jumble among the African species of the genus "Garra" and establish their present geographic distribution. Extensive field collections have been made from Ethiopian freshwater bodies where the diversity of the genus is believed to be relatively high. Available museum specimens have been investigated. Morphology and morphometries have been used to identify the species. According to preliminary results, twelve forms (species?) are recognized from Ethiopia, five of which are new. Four of the "forms" are found in six other African countries while the remaining eight are known only from Ethiopia. 'G. dembeensis' is the most abundant and widely distributed species found in 75% of the drainage basins of Ethiopia and in six other African countries. Seven other species of the genus are known to occur in ten other African countries. Generally, the genus has so far been reported from fifteen African countries. The range is from Ethiopia in the east to Guinea in the west and from Chad in the north to Tanzania in the south. The historical biogeography of the genus is controversial.

22018: Interest in fluctuating asymmetries, random deviations from perfect bilateral symmetry, has spread to studies of sexual selection because of the intriguing idea that females could use the degree of asymmetry of a male trait to assess the genetic quality of potential mates. The evidence that females prefer males with symmetrical sexual signals, however, has remained controversial. A problem that applies to most previous studies is that preference for trait size can be misinterpreted as preference for symmetry, even when overall trait size is held constant, if females assess trait size by the largest minimum on one side. If overall trait size is equal between males, the asymmetrical males will have the maximum and minimum trait size, and so preference to mate with symmetrical males could actually reflect a preference to avoid males with the minimum trait on one side. Xiphophorus cortezi females preferred males with symmetrical bar numbers when the minimum number of bars was held constant. The strength of female preference for the symmetrical males with fewer bars was negatively correlated with the strength of preference the same females had for bar number. These results clearly demonstrate that females preferred trait symmetry in addition to trait size.

22019: I tested for female preferences of male body size in zebrafish (Danio rerio). My experimental design allowed females to view a small and a large male in adjacent aquaria. Time that females spent near males was scored from 20 min replays of videos. The average standard length (SL) of large males was 28 mm and small males were 22 mm. The average difference between small and large male SL in individual experiments was 6.4 mm. Females spent significantly more time near large males (average = 647 s) than small males (average = 550 s; ind. t-test, P < 0.02). When female time near males was scored only if the males were adjacent to the female, females also spent significantly more time near large males (178 s) than near small males (117 s; ind. t-test, P < 0.05). My current experiments are to test for female preference of male yellow coloration by filtering out yellow light from experimental males, and to use DNA fingerprinting to identify paternity in competitive matings.

22020: Multiple-male mating by females and the resulting sperm competition are widespread in animals. Benefits accrued by males that inseminate many females include increased reproductive success. However, the reasons underlying multiple mating by females are ambiguous since a single insemination can fertilize all her ova and mating involves potential costs to both sexes. One such cost is an increased risk of predation. Recent studies have shown that animals can assess the local risk of predation and, in response to high risk, females may decrease their mate choosiness and males may increase their use of alternative mating tactics. If predation risk increases the relative frequency of sneaky copulations in males and reduces choosiness in females, then we predict a higher frequency of concurrent multiple paternity per brood in females originating from high-predation populations as compared to females from low-predation populations. To test this hypothesis, genetic data from a polymorphic microsatellite locus was employed to conservatively estimate multiple paternity in eight populations of the Trinidadian guppy (Poecilia reticulata) differing in fish predation regime. Our data suggest that, on average, the frequency of concurrent multiple paternity is three times greater in high-predation populations than in low-predation populations. These results further suggest that predation risk reduces the variance in male mating success and thus the opportunity for sexual selection within populations.

22021: Our observations of round goby nesting behaviour on shipwrecks in the western basin of Lake Erie using a video camera indicate that these fish spawn at much greater depths (7 m) than previously reported (< 2m). Of the species that approached the exposed nest (rock bass, smallmouth bass, yellow perch, logperch, round gobies), most behavioural interactions occurred between the guarding male and other round gobies. During 12 minutes of observation, there were 63 instances in which round gobies approached the nest and in 4 cases, intruders fed on eggs. In response, the guarding male approached (34 times), chased (18 times) and hit (4 times) round goby intruders. The response by the resident goby to the presence of rock bass (1 swam by and 7 approached) resulted in 6 approaches, 4 chases and 1 hit. The resident male responded to juvenile smallmouth bass (3 swam by and 1 approached) only once by approaching the intruder. The guarding male did not respond to either logperch or yellow perch. We anticipate that recruitment of round gobies will increase substantially in Lake Erie owing to the presence of artificial reefs (shipwrecks) and the ability of guarding males to defend nests effectively.

22022: Fundulus heteroclitus live in tidal creeks where predation risk varies with the structure of the microhabitat and time of year. Structure of the microhabitat varies as a function of the tides. Accurate recognition and response to predators is essential to the survival of prey. This study investigated alarm behavior of adult and juvenile estuarine fish, F. heteroclitus. Activity was determined in response to conspecific alarm chemical in relatively deep and shallow water (aquaria and fingerbowls). In deep water, in the fall, F. heteroclitus show container dependent alarm behavior. Both adult and juvenile fish showed a significant decrease in activity in response to alarm chemical compared addition of control. However, in shallow fingerbowls neither adults or juveniles show a decrease in activity. Adults also show seasonal context dependent alarm behavior. In winter adults in aquaria show no change in activity in response to alarm chemicals. Accurate responses to alarm chemicals may be those that are modulated by context, such as water depth, that reflects the actual risk of predation. Field experiments will determine if these results extend to the field.

22023: Diet studies often measure selectivity, or the proportion of diet made up by specific prey types compared to their occurrence in the environment. This measure is the result of two events: the choice to attack that prey type and whether the attack results in a successful capture. This study quantified these two events separately in the juveniles of three species of sculpin (Cottidae) to compare their roles in determining the taxonomic composition of the diet. Choice showed a greater influence on the occurrence of harpacticoid copepods and gammarid amphipods in the diet than performance. Significant interspecific differences in choice of harpacticoids and gammarids were found to be correlated with differences in the occurrence of these prey types in the diets of the three species. Performance played a greater role in determining the occurrence of calanoid copepods in the diet than did choice. Species and individuals with high capture success on calanoids did not choose to attack this prey type more often than those with lower capture success. This study indicates that classic measures of selectivity will only reflect active choice or avoidance when capture success on a prey type is high.

22024: Diel behavior was studied on pairs of adults living in burrows and juveniles sharing these burrows. Juveniles retire into burrows at dusk and emerge at dawn to break into large swarms, feeding on plankton as far as 10 m from their home burrow at depths 4 to 34 m. Adults clean their burrows by spitting out sand and carrying out rubble. At night neither adults nor juveniles emerge from their burrows. Burrow entrances were observed continuously for periods of 2 to 35 hours with low light and regular video cameras. Disturbances to their burrow entrances by other fish and a large octopus caused only a temporary break in their cleaning activity. Heads of adults emerged the most (1/3 of total length) and stayed out longest (1/2 min) when they were not cleaning out their burrows but appeared to look around or lunge at other fishes. They may cannibalize their young as food. The swimming and feeding behavior of juvenile P. leucotaenia (sometimes called "mimic catfish") do not resemble that of the venomous catfish, Plotosus lineatus. Sixteen reefs were surveyed at Guadalcanal, and the Florida, Russell, and New Georgia islands. P. leucotaenia were found in all except the isolated St. Marys Island.

22025: Marine fish assemblages may be viewed as being structured by deterministic or chaotic processes. To understand factors important in structuring an assemblage of four blenniid species (Family: Blenniidae) I collected data on their abundance and distribution in early July 1997 on six offshore petroleum platforms. Hurricane Danny passed through the study area 50 km offshore of the Louisiana coast in mid July. Between late August and mid-September I collected data on nine platforms in the same area. I conducted visual censuses on diagonal cross-members of the platforms at depths of 1, 5, 10, and 15 m. Blennies displayed a distinct vertical zonation with Scartella cristata confined to the upper 2 m and Parablennius marmoreus limited to 10-15 m depths. I used Morisita's index (Im) to investigate blenniid assemblage similarity among platforms and the effect of the hurricane. Im values were compared to a null model of randomly generated data. Platforms were similar in assemblage structure with three of the four depths sampled having average Im's > 1. Pre- and post-hurricane Im's averaged greater than one in three of the four depths sampled, indicating that this disturbance did not affect these blenniid assemblages.

22026: I studied near-shore, juvenile reef fishes associated with floating objects along the Pacific coast of Panama. Using naturally-occurring flotsam and Fish Aggregation Devices (FADs), I made observations and conducted experiments on factors affecting group size and species composition. Increased FAD size and the presence of fouling biota positively affected aggregation sizes and the number of fish species present. FADs hung with model fish, lead weights and unmanipulated control FADs did not differ significantly in aggregation size or composition. However, drifting FADs deployed with live fish (Abudefduf troschelii) appeared to recruit additional fish more than those deployed without fish. The species composition of aggregations associated with drifting flotsam differed from aggregations found with anchored flotsam and anchored FADs. At an array of anchored FADs, species composition was predictable over days to weeks, but showed distinct changes over a period of months.
Department of Biological Sciences, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ 86011-5640
22027: The phylogenetic intra-relationships of esocoid fishes have been examined repeatedly in systematic studies with contradictory results. The pre-Tertiary origin of the group and low Recent diversity likely contribute to the apparent paucity of apomorphic characters that define esocoid clades. Currently, the Esocoidei contains two families, the Esocidae and Umbridae, with Esox coextensive with Esocidae, and Dallia, Novumbra, and Umbra comprising the Umbridae. Generally, the following inter-generic relationships are accepted: (Esox (Novumbra (Dallia, Umbra))), but the literature abounds with conflicting evidence. Phylogenetic analyses of DNA sequence data from the 16S rRNA and cytochrome b mitochondrial genes strongly support a previously overlooked hypothesis of esocoid relationships. Parsimony and maximum likelihood analyses show a paraphyletic Umbridae in the following set of esocoid relationships: (Umbra (Dallia (Novumbra, Esox))). Published studies of esocoid karyotypes, allozymes, and fossils offer supporting evidence for the DNA-derived hypothesis. A survey of published data on esocoid anatomy may reveal previously unrecognized morphological synapomorphies to diagnose the newly postulated clades.
University of Washington Fish Collection, Box 355100, Seattle, WA 98195, USA
22028: Goodeine fishes are remarkable for the degree to which they provision developing embryos. A suite of physiological and morphological traits permits internal fertilization, pronounced matrotrophy, and live birth in this natural group from the central plateau of Mexico. Morphological and nucleic acid sequence (COI) data form the basis of a phylogenetic analysis of goodeid interrelationships. Forty-one species from 18 genera comprise the ingroup, and members of the Cyprinodontidae, Fundulidae, Poeciliidae, Profundulidae, and Oxyzygonectes are utilized as outgroups to polarize character states. Monophyly of the Goodeidae, and the sister-group relationship of the Goodeinae and Empetrichthyinae, is supported. The Profundulidae is supported as the sister-group to the Goodeidae. Early diversification events within the Goodeinae are not well supported, potentially indicating rapid radiation of the major lineages. The evolution and biogeography of the Goodeidae will be discussed.
Division of Fishes - UMMZ, University of Michigan, 1109 Geddes Ave., Ann Arbor, MI 48109-1079 USA
22029: Variation in trophic morphology is widespread in teleosts. The sources of this variation have been explored in a number of studies, and the genetic and environmental basis for extreme variation have been identified in a variety of fish. Here, I address the role development plays in producing phenotypic variation in a putative species complex of the Bahamian pupfish Cyprinodon. This taxon offers an excellent opportunity to address the origin of morphological variation in closely related species, because sympatrically occurring Cyprinodon exhibit a striking diversity in feeding morphology and behavior, yet putative species show only partial reproductive isolation. Offspring from three species and their hybrids were bred in the lab, and ontogenetic trajectories of their feeding morphology were followed until maturity. In Cyprinodon, very small differences in growth rates translate into large differences in feeding morphology. This developmental program has implications for large-scale, macroevolutionary patterns.
Corson Hall, Ecology and Systematics, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853-2701 USA
22030: The systematics and taxonomic history of the genus Sorubim (Teleostei: Pimelodidae) is unclear because of confusing and inadequate descriptive taxonomic literature. To assess the taxonomic status of species in the genus, I examined 347 specimens for morphological variation, including analysis of morphometry, meristics, osteology, and pigmentation throughout the known geographic range. An extensive literature review of the ten named species allocated to Sorubim and analysis of morphological data support the recognition of four species: Sorubim lima, widespread in the Amazon, Parana, and Orinoco basins; S. elongatus n. sp., occurring in the Essequibo, Orinoco, and upper Amazon drainages; S. caudacuspis n. sp., endemic to the Rio Magdalena and Lago Maracaibo drainages in Northwestern South America; and S. trigonocephalus, known only from the Rio Tapajos region in Brazil. The taxonomic revision presented includes a redescription of the genus, recognition of two nominal species as valid, descriptions of two new species, a dichotomous key, and distributional data for all nominal forms. Because of the small sample sizes available for S. trigonocephalus, future study of this species is warranted. All species of Sorubim are significant components of the ornamental fish trade and frequently found in local markets as a source of subsistence protein.
Southern Illinois University, Dept. of Zoology, Carbondale, IL 62901-6501
22031: The superfamily Poecilioidea contains approximately 300 species of fishes in two families, the Anablepidae (13 spp.) and the Poeciliidae (approx. 287 spp.). The monophyly of this superfamily has been supported by previous studies using morphology and DNA sequence data. However, the phylogenetic relationships within the group have been controversial. This phylogenetic analysis of over 90 transformation series and 30 representative poecilioid species supports the monophyly of the two included families. The poeciliine tribes Heterandrini, Poeciliini, and Cnesterodontini as traditionally recognized are shown to be nonmonophyletic. The facultatively viviparous species Tomeurus gracilis is nested within the poeciliine tribe Cnesterodontini and represents an evolutionary loss of obligate viviparity. Based on the phylogeny, the genus Aplocheilichthys should be restricted to the type species, Aplocheilichthys spilauchen, and Micropanchax should be recognized as the valid genus for most of the species previously placed in Aplocheilichthys. The evolution of viviparity and pelagic lacustrine habits in this group will be discussed.
Natural History Museum, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS 66045-2454 USA
22032: Snubnose darters are a fascinating group of fishes in the genus Etheostoma; breeding males exhibit some of the most fantastic colors found in North American fishes. The results of an analysis of complete cytochrome b DNA sequences (1140 base pairs) for 32 species of snubnose darters and putative close relatives are presented. Topologies obtained with parsimony, distance, and maximum likelihood criteria are congruent. The phylogenetic hypothesis supports relationships within snubnose darters that are corroborated with other evidence, although it differs from previous hypotheses in basal relationships. The cytochrome b gene tree suggests that snubnose darters are polyphyletic, with members of the subgenus Etheostoma s.s. related to one clade, and that members of the E. variatum species group are not closely related to snubnose darters or to Etheostoma s.s. The phylogeny is used for studying the evolution of several male breeding color characters that were coded and mapped onto the tree, and sexual selection experiments determined that these breeding colors were important to male reproductive success. This combination of evidence is used to propose a role for sexual selection in the differentiation of snubnose darter lineages and species.
Illinois Natural History Survey, 607 East Peabody Drive, Champaign, IL 61820, USA
22033: The perciform suborder Gobioidei contains an estimated 2000 species in 270 genera, found throughout the world oceans and freshwaters. This lineage is very diverse and reductive evolution is common, making traditional morphological systematic studies particularly difficult. In an attempt to resolve relationships among gobioid groups, I sequenced a 2022 base pair fragment of the mitochondrial genome, comprising the entire ND1 and ND2 genes for 40 gobioid species and performed phylogenetic analysis using cladistic parsimony methods. My data set includes representatives of the Gobiidae (including all subfamilies: Gobiinae, Gobionellinae, Oxudercinae, Amblyopinae and Sicydiinae), Microdesmidae (both subfamilies: Microdesminae and Ptereleotrinae), Kraemeriidae and Schindleriidae; representatives of the Eleotrididae were used as outgroup taxa. Analysis of the nucleotide data yielded a single phylogeny for which Bremer support and jackknife indices indicated weaker support in the deeper nodes. Analysis of translated amino acid data yielded two phylogenies differing only in the placement of one taxon; this phylogeny is congruent in many respects with gobioid relationships suggested by morphological characters. My analysis provides a broad view of gobioid relationships and, in particular, provides evidence for the relationships of the paedomorphic Kraemeriidae and Schindleriidae within the Gobioidei.
Museum of Zoology, Division of Fishes, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109 USA
22034: The monophyly of the rhamphichthyoid gymnotiforms is supported by previous phylogenetic studies of gymnotiform fishes. In contrast, the status and relationships of the constituent subgroups of the rhamphichthyoids remain poorly understood. The goal of this work was to determine whether the currently recognized rhamphichthyoid taxa represent monophyletic groups and to ascertain the species-level relationships among them, with special emphasis on the Family Hypopomidae Mago-Leccia, 1976. An additional goal was to gain insight into the evolution of the species-specific electric organ discharge (EOD). A phylogenetic study of 23 rhamphichthyoid species was carried out based on mitochondrial DNA sequence data from the portions of the 12S rRNA, 16S rRNA and cytochrome b genes and a morphological data set. Results indicate that nominal hypopomid genera Steatogenys and Hypopygus do not form a clade with other nominal hypopomids but strongly support the monophyly of the remaining nominal hypopomids. Additionally, the nominal species of Brachyhypopomus form a clade with five new species. Genus Brachyhypopomus is the sister taxon to the monotypic genus Microstemarchus which together form the sister group to genus Hypopomus. Complex EODs and a monophasic EOD appear to have arisen within the Hypopomidae independently of these character states in outgroup taxa.
Cornell University, Division of Biological Sciences, Section of Neurobiology and Behavior, Ithaca, NY 14853, USA
22035: The Amphiprioninae is a subfamily of marine fishes, commonly called anemonefishes, composed of two genera (Amphiprion and Premnas) with approximately 28 species. The phylogenetic relationships within this subfamily are poorly understood. Although a hypothetical set of relationships has been previously proposed, the phylogeny of the group has never been fully examined. Previous work has suggested that the members of this subfamily are divided among six species complexes. At least one representative species from all six of these complexes and three outgroup (pomacentrid) genera were examined. Morphological characters, primarily osteological ones, were used to conduct a phylogenetic analysis of this subfamily. The preliminary results will be presented and evolution of the fish-anemone relationship will be discussed.
Natural History Museum, University of Kansas, Lawrence, KS 66045-2454 USA
22036: Hypotheses concerning modes of allopatric speciation make explicit predictions regarding patterns of phylogenetic and biogeographic diversification. This investigation will test allopatric speciation models using phylogenetic and biogeographic information for the subgenus Swainia, a monophyletic group of four described species in the genus Percina. Complete gene sequences of the mitochondrially encoded cytochrome b have been collected from all species of Swainia, including individuals from multiple populations of P. phoxocephala and P. nasuta. Patterns of nucleotide variation were investigated and phylogenetic relationships were estimated using maximum parsimony, maximum likelihood, and distance optimality criteria. Heterogeneity of nucleotide substitution rate was examined using both maximum parsimony relative rate tests and a likelihood ratio test. Inferred phylogenetic relationships, biogeographic patterns, and relative amounts of nucleotide divergence are used to develop hypotheses of speciation in Swainia.
22037: This presentation is part of a wider study of the biogeography of Australian freshwater fishes. Southeastern Australia is hereby defined as coastal drainages from the Fitzroy River through Gulf of St. Vincent, including the inland Murray system separated from coastal drainages by the Great Dividing Range. It has the following biogeographic relationships of fishes restricted to freshwater: 1) 5 of 8 species from southern Victoria also occur in the Murray system; and 2) 18 of 27 species (or species pairs) co-occur between coastal Queensland drainages and the Murray system. The relationships of an additional 6 species endemic to the Murray system are more obscure. Biogeographic connectivity between the Murray and surrounding drainages thus appears high. Past biogeographic explanations for these relationships have relied heavily upon river captures, making faunal distributions easily explained. However, the last 15 years have seen a paradigm shift in the proposed evolution of the Great Dividing Range including evidence that river captures are either non-existent or very old (> 30-60 mya). Most patterns are congruent with present geological scenarios although exceptions exist. The new geologic conclusions are assessed on the basis of biological evidence and new hypotheses are provided to explain present distribution patterns.
Biology Department, Arizona State University, Tempe AZ 85287-1501, USA
22038: Phylogenetic relationships of the endemic Malagasy cichlids were investigated using DNA sequence data and combined evidence. Prior attempts based on morphological evidence to generate a highly supported and resolved phylogenetic hypothesis have been only partially successful, and this lack of resolution has been attributed to muted anatomical variation and a high degree of convergence/parallelism within Cichlidae. DNA sequence data is presented corresponding to two regions of the mitochondrial genome for a representative sampling of cichlid taxa, including all of the known Malagasy cichlids. The use of molecular sequence data results in a highly resolved phylogenetic hypothesis for Cichlidae. However, support for higher-level relationships is relatively weak, and may indicate that differentiation in ancient cichlid lineages occurred over a relatively short time. Results based on DNA sequence data indicate that the Malagasy cichlids (including the Asian genera) are not monophyletic, that the Etropline cichlids (Etroplus from India/Sri Lanka and Paretroplus from Madagascar) form a natural group, and that the Ptychochromine cichlids (including Oxylapia) are a monophyletic Malagasy assemblage. Biogeography of the Malagasy cichlids, and Cichlidae in general, will also be discussed.
Museum of Zoology, Fish Division, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109-1079 USA
22039: An amphibian survey was initiated at Brazos Bend State Park, Fort Bend County, Texas to assess anecdotal observations of anuran population declines. From February to July 1997, 12 amphibian species were documented at the park. Sixty-nine sites used by amphibians were identified, of which 73% contained evidence of breeding. It does not appear that amphibian species are in decline at Brazos Bend State Park. In February 1998, 350 meters of PVC pipe were installed at selected sites to evaluate the effectiveness of this technique in regard to hylid frog populations. These and other sites are currently being monitored in order to gain insight to amphibian population dynamics at Brazos Bend State Park.
22040: Apparent declines of amphibian populations in many parts of the world have caused great concern in recent years. This study was conducted to determine what effects agriculturally induced fragmentation of forests has had on amphibian assemblages and their distribution in a midwestern landscape. Potential breeding pools and upland areas in 30 forest patches of various sizes and degrees of isolation were intensively sampled for amphibians from April through August 1996 and March through August 1997. Species presence was documented by using pitfall trapping, anuran vocalization surveys, cover board sampling, minnow traps, and dipnetting for larva. Amphibian, anuran and salamander assemblages were all nonrandomly distributed across the landscape. Bufo americanus and Hyla versicolor were ubiquitous whereas the distribution of several species including Ambystoma tigrinum, A. texanum, Plethodon cinereus, Rana clamitans, and R. pipiens showed significant nesting. Overall, species richness was significantly associated with a weighted measure of wetland permanency (WETWGT, p=0.0001, WETWGTC2, p=0.0029), with forest patches which have seasonal and semi-permanent wetlands containing more species. Abundance of amphibians was significantly associated with forest proximity (LOGPR, p=0.0001, LOGPRC2, p=0.0037), with more isolated patches having greater amphibian abundance. The observed distribution and degree of nestedness exhibited by several amphibians suggests that these species respond to landscape-level factors.

22041: The longleaf pine ecosystem, once widespread in the southeastern United States, has been reduced by as much as 98%. Restoration of this endangered ecosystem can be a mechanism for conservation, in an attempt to reverse existing damage and create more resilient communities. Restoration methods implemented in sandhills must be based in a deep knowledge of the ecosystem to effectively recreate and manage all aspects. Consequently, restoration success can only be evaluated by examining community response. Since reptiles and amphibians occupy the ecosystem at a fairly small scale, these communities may be important indicators of microhabitat restoration success. Previous work on herpetofaunal response to disturbance regimes has demonstrated the complexity of the effects and the importance of habitat structure. Habitat requirements for sandhill herpetofauna are very diverse, demonstrating the need to closely examine these communities when making management decisions. My study, focused on reptiles and amphibians, is one portion of a multi-agency investigation of three sandhill restoration techniques on Eglin Air Force Base, Florida: fire, oak-specific herbicide, and mechanical oak felling. Pitfall traps and drift fences were used to capture reptiles and amphibians in restoration treatment areas, control plots and 'typical' longleaf pine sandhill areas during the summer of 1997. Animals were identified to species, marked, sexed, weighed, measured, and visually examined. Vegetative cover data were also collected. The objective of this project is to examine herpetofaunal species richness and abundance, as well as population age class structure and sex ratios, with regards to the restoration treatment and vegetative structure.
Department of Wildlife Ecology and Conservation, University of Florida, Box 110430, Gainesville, FL 32611-430
22042: Alberta-Pacific Forest Industries Inc. (AL-PAC) operates a large pulp mill in the mixed-wood boreal forest of northeastern Alberta. The company harvests within its 6,000,000 ha Forest Management Area (FMA) using an 'ecosystem management' perspective. In other words, AL-PAC attempts to mimic fire, the dominant natural disturbance of the boreal forest. Five amphibian species, including two that appear to have undergone population declines, occur in the FMA. In 1997, I sampled anuran communities at 12 lakes to investigate whether each species showed the same relative abundance in logged, naturally burned, and undisturbed areas. I employed call surveys, transect sampling, egg and larval searches, and metamorph searches. Additionally, I conducted vegetation surveys on each transect to quantitatively examine differences in habitat. Preliminary results suggest that lakes with adjacent cutblocks support the highest number of amphibians; however, this may be a function of lake size, distance from active roads, or forest type. An analysis to separate these effects is underway.
Department of Biology, University of Victoria, PO Box 3020 STN CSC, Victoria BC V8W 3N5, Canada
22043: Human activities tend to create highly fragmented landscapes, thereby exposing animal populations to edges. I am interested in the impacts of forest-pasture edges on the dynamics of frog and lizard populations. Using a paired-plot design I described the abundance and distribution of lizards (Norops spp.) and leaf-litter frogs (Eleutherodactylus spp.) in 10 forest fragments near Las Cruces, Costa Rica. The study took place from February to June 1997 and covered both dry and wet seasons. No species was definitively absent from the edge plots. Nocturnal leaf-litter frogs were generally equally abundant near forest edges and in forest interiors. The single diurnal eleutherodactylid species, however, was consistently more abundant in the forest interiors, suggesting that edge effects may be stronger during the day than at night. Anoline lizards were more abundant at the edges during the dry season but became more abundant in forest interiors during the wet season. This seasonal variation adds a new dimension to our understanding of edge effects, and carries important practical implications for future studies. The reproductive period of the lizards, which coincides with the rainy season, as well as lower rates of parasitism on anoline lizards near edges, are offered as possible explanations for the observed seasonal pattern.
Department of Natural Resources, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853-3001, USA
22044: Terrestrial salamanders spend the majority of their time in cool, moist refugia underground, but must surface to forage and breed. Although little is known about their surface activity patterns, abundance is usually inferred by counts of surface active salamanders on wet nights. Recently, such counts have been used to assess the impacts of timber harvesting on terrestrial salamanders. It is assumed in these studies that the percent of the population active on the surface is not altered by the treatment. We tested this assumption by conducting a mark-recapture study on harvested and control plots. We found significantly different proportions active between treatments. At one location, the harvested plot had a lower percent active than its control (Plethodon cinereus: 4.0% vs. 9.2%, p=.021; P. glutinosus: 3.8% vs. 11.7%, p=.091). At the other location, the harvested plots had a higher percent active than their controls (P. cinereus: 4.2% and 3.9% vs. 1.6% and 1.3%, p=.017). At this site, surface counts indicated there were more salamanders on the harvested plots than on the controls, but mark-recapture estimates indicated there were actually twice as many salamanders on the control plots.

22045: Populations that experience a large reduction in effective size are expected to exhibit a bottleneck effect which will include loss of heterozygosity and loss of alleles. Populations of the southwestern pond turtle, Clemmys marmorata pallida, in Central and Southern California were impacted by an extended drought that occurred from 1987-1992 and exhibited local population size decreases up to 85% during this period. I examined changes in genetic diversity in four populations of C. marmorata in the drought affected area by comparing microsatellite DNA allele frequencies from tissue samples collected before and after this drought period. Genotypes of five microsatellite loci were determined to assess the genetic diversity within these samples. Heterozygosity was used as a measurement of genetic diversity. Although no significant decline in heterozygosity was shown in the five loci, there was a decrease in the number of alleles present in the most severely impacted population. Since most individuals that were present in the post-drought samples were survivors of the drought, the first sign of decreased genetic diversity would be the loss of alleles. Changes in the level of genetic diversity (heterozygosity) would only be detectable in subsequent post-drought generations.

22046: An amphibian survey was initiated at Brazos Bend State Park, Fort Bend County, Texas to assess anecdotal observations of anuran population declines. From February to July 1997, 12 amphibian species were documented at the park. Sixty-nine sites used by amphibians were identified, of which 73% contained evidence of breeding. These and other sites are currently being monitored in order to gain insight to amphibian population dynamics at Brazos Bend State Park.
22047: The geographic range of the gopher tortoise has declined due to habitat destruction and fragmentation. Protection strategies typically include preserving patches of habitat or conserving areas occupied by tortoises, even if those areas are restricted in size and quality. However, the patterns observed in these sites can differ from those in large, contiguous areas where conditions may more closely resemble those under which the species evolved. We tracked 131 tortoises via radio-telemetry for one year on an 11,700 ha longleaf pine reserve in southwest Georgia. Male tortoises utilized an average of 9.3 + 4.6 burrows and traveled an average total distance of 83.7 + 73.8 m during the study period. Females utilized 4.8 ± 2.4 burrows and traveled 48.2 ± 57.7 m. The longest movements were 6.4 km by a male tortoise and 480 m by a female. The results of this study emphasize the need to preserve large, contiguous habitats for use by gopher tortoises. Furthermore, it suggests that movement by tortoises is limited in small habitats, especially those surrounded by vast inhospitable areas. Data gathered within large study sites may provide better information for the long-term preservation of this species.

22048: Mitochondrial DNA sequence analyses were used to infer phylogeographic relationships among individuals of the lizard species Cnemidophorus sexlineatus, as well as to determine whether a population of C. sexlineatus in Michigan is endemic or recently introduced. Individuals were obtained from Colorado, Oklahoma, Indiana, Michigan, and Florida. A PCR generated fragment which spans the mtDNA ND3 to ND4 gene region, and including the Arginine tRNA, was sequenced for each individual. Sceloporus grammicus and C. gularis sequences were used as outgroups. The preliminary data cannot rule out the possibility that the Michigan population is endemic. The Florida individuals are in a clade basal to a clade that contains Michigan, Indiana, and Oklahoma individuals. Sequence divergence values of the Michigan specimens range from 1.2% to 5.8%. The Indiana and Oklahoma specimens have sequence divergence values of 1.6% to 2.3% and 1.1% to 1.5% respectively. One Colorado sample forms a clade with the C. gularis sample, its sequence divergence is 8.3%.

22049: Peatlands are increasingly exploited in Europe and North America due to the demand for peat in horticulture. As a result, these wetlands are threatened, particularly in New Brunswick and Quebec, North America's principal peat producers. I used drift fences and pitfall traps to investigate amphibian populations in pristine bogs and disturbed bogs (i.e., bog remnants adjacent to peat harvesting operations) of southeastern New Brunswick. Results following 20,592 trap nights indicate that species richness is higher in pristine bogs than disturbed bogs (range 2-7 spp.). Rana clamitans was the only species sensitive to peat harvesting, while the abundance of Rana sylvatica, Rana pipiens, Bufo americanus americanus and Rana septentrionalis did not differ between pristine bogs and bog fragments. Captured individuals consisted almost exclusively of ranid juveniles in both types of bogs. These data show that peat bog harvesting has a definite influence on adjacent amphibian communities. However, additional work will be needed to differentiate natural population fluctuations from the impacts of peat harvesting on amphibian movements and resource (i.e., bog ponds) utilization.

22050: For amphibians that breed in temporary pools, juvenile dispersal is an important life history movement linking the aquatic habitat of larvae to the surrounding forest habitat occupied by most adults. We examined whether selection occurs for closed-canopy conditions during dispersal using pitfall traps and drift fences to sample naturally occurring, upland populations of wood frogs (Rana sylvatica) and spotted salamanders (Ambystoma maculatum) along recently created forest-clearcut edges in central Maine. Habitat preferences during dispersal were further investigated using an experimental approach that quantified the movements of newly metamorphosed wood frogs cultured in artificial pools located along an abrupt forest-powerline edge. Among natural populations the abundance of juveniles and adults of both species declined sharply across a gradient running from relatively mature forest-interior habitat (70-90 years old) to recently clearcut habitat (2-11 years old). Similarly, in the powerline experiment, juvenile wood frogs showed a dispersal preference for closed-canopy habitat immediately upon metamorphosis, with the highest capture rates occurring in microhabitats characterized by dense foliage in both the understory and canopy layers. Our results suggest that populations of wood frogs, spotted salamanders, and other vernal pool breeding amphibian species are likely to benefit from efforts to maintain connectivity between upland forest habitats and aquatic breeding sites.

22051: Bison wallows and intermittent streams were sampled weekly in spring 1996 and 1997 on Konza Prairie Research Natural Area, Kansas. We monitored water chemistry and development of western chorus frogs (Pseudacris triseriata) as these aquatic habitats dried. Abiotic factors temporally were more variable in bison wallows than in intermittent streams even after flow stopped. Dissolved oxygen and ammonium fluctuated diurnally in wallows, but remained stable in intermittent streams until just before drying. Water temperature and pH were correlated negatively to water volume in wallows, but not in streams. Eggs in bison wallows hatched at Gosner stages 21 and 22 within 4 to 8 days after laying, whereas eggs in intermittent streams hatched in 14 days at about Gosner stage 21. The majority of tadpoles in wallows reached Gosner stages 38 to 42 in 6 weeks, when wallows dried. In contrast, tadpole development in streams progressed no further than stage 25 until flow ceased in streams, and no tadpoles developed beyond stage 41 when the streams dried after 16 weeks. Differences in developmental rates of these frogs likely result from differences in water temperature and chemistry between ephemeral aquatic habitats found in wallows and streams.
Division of Biology, 232 Ackert Hall, Kansas State University, Manhattan, Kansas 66506 USA
22052: The post-breeding migration of Rana temporaria was studied by means of radio tracking over three years. One site consisted of an extensive ungrazed, uncut moist meadow where suitable foraging habitats and the breeding site were all contiguous with each other, while in another site suitable habitats were separated by cultivated fields. The study period of the first year coincided with a drought, while the study periods of the following two years had above normal precipitation. This enabled a factorial analysis of the effects of seasonal weather, landscape type and sex on migratory behavior. In the farmland site and during the wet years frogs moved farther from their breeding pond and sources of open water, changed position more often and made longer movements when position was changed. In the farmland site frogs also migrated farther and did so more directly. Nearly all differences between sites were more noticeable during the wet year. There were no significant differences between the sexes, neither were any of the differences between habitats or wet and dry years sex dependent. These migration patterns are discussed in terms of the effects of habitat fragmentation on species survival and the consequences for dispersal between breeding populations.
Ecology Building, Lund University, 223 62 Lund, Sweden
22053: The influence of weather on salamander breeding activity has been well documented. However, weather influence on specific movement patterns is not yet well understood. I investigated the influence of weather variables on movements of Northwestern salamanders. Radio-tracking was conducted during the winter when this species is most active. Both non-breeding and breeding migration movements were observed. Movements were significantly correlated with both temperature increase and rain onset. This relationship was strongest when a cold, dry period was followed by a warm, wet period. Movements began when daily temperatures rose above a mean of 5°C and a minimum of 0°C, and more than 20mm of rain had fallen within the last 24 hours. During these periods most radio-tagged salamanders moved within 48 hours of the weather change and of each other. Breeding migration movements were also correlated with this type of weather change and migration onset invariably began within 48 hours of the first winter thaw. Subsequent cold, dry periods were observed to temporarily suspend migrational movements. During extended periods of warm rainy weather, correlations between weather variables and movements were much weaker and tended to be better explained by individual salamander movement frequency patterns.

22054: Nitrogen pollution from anthropogenic sources enters water bodies through runoff associated with nitrate fertilization, livestock, precipitation, and effluents from industrial, human and animal wastes. This review assesses the potential for nitrate to affect amphibian populations by comparing environmental concentrations of nitrate in North American waters to nitrate concentrations known to cause toxicity to captive amphibians and other species that play an important role in amphibian ecology. Lethal and sublethal effects in amphibians are detected at nitrate concentrations between 2.5 and 100 mg/L. We found environmental concentrations of nitrate in watersheds throughout North America from <1 to >100 mg/L. Furthermore, amphibian food (insects) and predators (fish) are also affected by these elevated levels of nitrate in surface waters. From this we conclude that nitrate concentrations in watersheds in North America are high enough to cause death and developmental anomalies in amphibians. In the interim, use of vegetated buffer strips adjacent to water courses can reduce nitrogen contamination of surface waters. Ultimately, there is a need to reduce the use of fertilizers, control the run-off of human and livestock waste and establish and enforce water quality guidelines for nitrate for the protection of aquatic life.

22056: Billings reservoir (127 km2, 23° 42' - 23° 45'S; 46° 27' - 46° 22'W) is the largest water body in the metropolitan region of São Paulo (Brazil). Its building started in 1925 in order to supply the city of São Paulo with electricity. During many years it presented low environmental quality due to the reception of organic sewage from the metropolitan region. Nowadays, it has multiple uses. An intense artisanal fishery activity is present, with 191 fishermen. Landings were recorded daily during a year (1996). The dominance of Nile tilapia is attributable to a combination of factors as ability to consume plankton and tolerance to low dissolved oxygen contents. 22057: Floodplain fishes in the mid-upper Rio Negro are exploited as ornamental fishes to provide subsistence to 3000 people in Barcelos, Amazonas (pop. 12,000; area 122,490 km2). Turtles and their eggs are the second most important protein resource, next to fish. This fishery constitutes over 60% of the economic activity of the region. About 60 species and 20 million fishes are captured for the trade annually. A single species, the cardinal tetra (Paracheirodon axelrodi), made up more than 70% of the catch. Over fishing in some areas may be attributed to lack of rural employment since other extractive economies have collapsed. Thus more people are involved in the fishery. El Niño, now, as in 1982-3, is probably the principal cause of the drastic decline of the fishery. Our goals are to understand the biology of this community so that a management plan can be devised to use these resources on a sustainable level. To accomplish these goals we are studying the biodiversity and biology of the species of fish used in the ornamental fish trade, the turtles used as food and trade, and the social-economic aspects of this fishery. It may be possible to use this resource as well as preserve it.
22058: Selective timber harvesting (removal of individual trees or small groups of trees), which creates gaps in the forest canopy, is widely practiced in public and private forests. Distributions of individual salamanders were determined by searching 1 m x 1 m quadrats along transects extending from the center of gaps into the surrounding forest. In the first year following harvest, we found that salamander distributions did not indicate significant movement from or avoidance of gap sites. However, salamander densities were somewhat elevated on the edges of gaps. Data for the second year following harvest are being analyzed.

22059: We entered citation information for all natural history and geographic distribution records from Herpetological Review (HR), from its first issues to the present. Citations include authors, species, keywords, and locality information. The HR database is available to anyone with WWW access, and can be searched in a variety of ways. 22060: The south-west coast of Australia (Darling Botanical District), as defined by the 800mm isohyet, has an area of some 160,000 square kilometres and 19 distinct river drainage basins. In comparison to habitats of southeastern Australia and the Northern Hemisphere, southwestern Australia has a much reduced aquatic faunal diversity: the freshwaters of this region contain only 10 species of native fishes, of which eight are endemic. With the exception of Tandanus bostocki (a freshwater catfish) none of these species typically exceed 140mm in total length. This very low number of freshwater fish species in southwestern Australian waters is thought to be a result of the regions arid past climate, insular nature, low and relatively featureless topography, and low productivity of its aquatic habitats. The regions recreational freshwater fishery currently comprises the introduced perch (Perca fluviatilis) and trouts (Salmo trutta, Oncorhynchus mykiss), and the native decapod, Cherax tenuimanus, the third largest freshwater crayfish. Preliminary data suggests the temperate climate of the south-west promotes fast growth-rates of perch, yet shortens the period during which their spawning is successful, relative to Northern Hemisphere populations. This paper also discusses the likely impact of P. fluviatilis on the established C. tenuimanus fishery, given that at times P. fluviatilis preys almost exclusively on this crayfish species.
22061: The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation has been directing the NY Amphibian and Reptile Atlas, a state-wide, ten-year survey of the herpetofaunal populations which relies heavily on volunteer participation. The web page (www.cortland.edu/herp/) contains identification keys and photographs of local species, information about the Atlas, and web resource links. 22062: In 1992, the Canadian government passed amendments to the Pulp and Paper Effluent Regulations (PPER) under the Fisheries Act, which included a requirement for mills to conduct an Environmental Effects Monitoring (EEM) program. 22063: Avon Park Air Force Range is a federal military reservation occupying 42,900 hectares in Florida's Greater Everglades Region. 22064: Diet and feeding habits of the smooth dogfish (Mustelus canis), Atlantic sharpnose shark (Rhizoprionodon terranovae), dusky shark (Carcharhinus obscurus) and the sand tiger (Carcharias taurus) were investigated through analysis of stomach contents. Diet in M. canis was relatively homogeneous and was dominated by crustaceans, consisting mostly of rock crabs, Cancer irroratus. 22065: Long-term field studies of sexual selection in the explosively breeding American toad, Bufo americanus, reveal only weak evidence of non-random mating based on size. Although advantages may accrue to females that breed with larger males, levels of male-male competition and opportunities for female choice vary. High levels of natal philopatry predict that close inbreeding should be common. Genetic analyses suggest to the contrary that: (1) in natural populations toads largely avoid close inbreeding, and (2) males' advertisement calls encode information about their genetic identities. To examine whether females can assess their relatedness to males by hearing their calls, I conducted laboratory playback experiments. The responses of female subjects to males' calls, broadcast alternately, were analysed as a function of their relatedness to each of the males (determined by multilocus DNA fingerprinting). Females discriminated between calls based on kinship, consistently orienting toward calls of the genetically less similar male. Responses were similar to field-recorded calls and to synthesised calls (controlling for call duration and number of pulses). Females showed no preference if equally related to each calling male. These results suggest that mate choice is more strongly influenced by selection to avoid close inbreeding than by sexual selection for other characters.

22066: Studies employing historical methods have shown that preexisting biases in the sensory systems of females are capable of driving the evolution of male traits. I used artificial neural network models - computer simulations emulating real nervous systems - to test whether receiver biases could be directly influenced by the evolutionary history of the female sensory apparatus. Neural networks were given an evolutionary history approximating that of the tungara frog, or one of various control histories. I found that not only does evolutionary history influence receiver biases, but that networks with a history approximating that of the tungara frog were best at predicting female responses to many novel heterospecific calls. The neural networks demonstrate patterns of preference that are clearly vestiges of past selection pressures, and make novel predictions about the preferences of real females.

22067: We have been using the advertisement call system of tungara frogs (Physalaemus pustulosus) and their close relatives to attempt to understand the evolution of communication systems. We have analyzed the advertisement calls and phylogenetic relationships of members of the Physalaemus pustulosus species group and three other congeners as outgroups. Using these data we have estimated calls at ancestral nodes and tested tungara frog female preferences for these calls. Here we address the following questions: (1) How conservative is the evolution of various call characters; (2) How do individual call characters influence advertisement call recognition (heterospecific call versus white noise) and discrimination (heterospecific call versus conspecific call); and, (3) Does the degree of plesiomorphy of a call character differentially influence call recognition and discrimination. Our results suggest that: (1) calls do not evolve as tightly coordinated suites of characters, but instead are arrays of more or less plesiomorphic or derived characters; (2) that call discrimination and recognition might be influenced differently by some call characters than others; and, (3) that the degree of plesiomorphy of a call character might have some effect on these tasks.
