22068: Visual displays are known in both intra- and intersexual anuran communication. We compare the patterns of visual signaling among seven anuran families and discuss the ecological contexts in which they may have evolved. We classified visual cues used during intraspecific interactions as discrete character states and mapped them onto a phylogenetic tree based on morphological characters. Groups of behavioural patterns are apparent and closely but not exclusively associated with anuran families. By adding ecological characteristics and geographic distributions of the involved species to the matrix, the resulting patterns suggest visual displays to be more similar between species of the same family. As striking exceptions, similar displays are performed by two across-family groups of species. Diurnal, neotropical leaf-litter inhabitants and mainly aposematic species in the Brachycephalidae, Bufonidae and Dendrobatidae exhibit an impressive variety of visual displays involving predominantly anterior parts of the body. Stream-side breeding, cryptic species in the Leptodactylidae, Myobatrachidae, Hylidae and Ranidae constitute another probably convergent group, which includes both nocturnal and diurnal species exposed to constant high ambient noise levels. They perform conspicuous visual displays by extending or 'flagging' the posterior limbs. However, Hyla parviceps and Phyllomedusa spp., which advertise and breed at ponds, perform similar displays. The observed patterns suggest that complex visual communication may have evolved under two ecological scenarios. One is associated with the shift to diurnality and the other with breeding at tropical mountain streams. 22069: Influence of time of day, location of shark and tracker experience on swimming speed was examined in seven subadult lemon sharks using speed sensing transmitters. 22070: Environmental contamination with anthropogenic chemicals has been implicated in the decline and disappearance of amphibians from many localities around the world. 22071: This study will explore the efficiency of different inventory sampling methods for an assemblage of lowland tropical amphibians and reptiles. 22072: Counts of amphibians over time were compiled from published accounts. At the time this abstract was written, 37 studies have yielded 110 separate count series for 45 amphibian species. 22074: As part of a long-term amphibian monitoring program, automated acoustical recorders were placed at five sites in two national parks in New Brunswick during the summer of 1997. 22075: Onondaga Lake lies in the Syracuse NY urbanization zone surrounded by industrial, commercial, and residential areas. 22076: The herpetofaunal community of a slash pine flatwoods ecosystem of north-central Florida was monitored from August 1993 through August 1994, October 1995 through September 1996, and November 1996 onward. 22077: Many of Ontario's amphibian species occur in forested areas of the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence region. 22078: The jargon of statistical power has invaded the vocabulary of almost every conservation biologist despite being largely absent from the literature as applied methodology. With respect to amphibian population monitoring, power refers to the probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis (that there is no decline) when the alternative hypothesis is true (a decline is occurring). Clearly we want high power in our monitoring programs so as to minimize the chance of making a Type II error (i.e., failing to detect a decline that is occurring). However, many amphibian monitoring programs likely do not have the necessary power to satisfactorily reduce the possibility that actual declines are occurring, even though some studies suggest stability and have data-sets that exceed 10 years. Here, we review the concepts of statistical power as they apply to detecting population declines. We then calculate an estimate of power for long-term data on bullfrogs (Rana catesbeiana) and wood frogs (Rana sylvatica) to investigate the problems associated with maximizing power in amphibian monitoring programs. We also comment on how an understanding of power should influence both the design of monitoring programs and management expectations.

22079: Previous amphibian relocation, repatriation, and translocation programs have proven most successful when introducing individuals in early developmental stages. Over the next 2 years, we will introduce egg masses of target amphibian species into artificial ponds in mitigated and existing wetland areas at Rocky Gap State Park. The shallow ponds will facilitate establishment of small, less abundant anuran species by excluding larger species with longer developmental stages. To monitor migration all ponds are encircled by drift fencing with both pitfall and funnel traps. Introduced egg masses will be monitored by recording percent hatching success and larvae will be monitored by tracking tadpole survivorship via weekly population estimates using a quadrat box sampling technique. Metamorphosed individuals captured while dispersing from the ponds will be marked with toe-clipping to determine if they return to breed in subsequent seasons. Additional constructed ponds in adjacent areas are being monitored for unaided colonization.

22080: Forming a large eastern embayment on Lake Huron, Georgian Bay comprises a body of water approximately the same size as the state of Vermont. Bounded in the west by the limestone arc of the Niagara escarpment, and in the east by the Canadian Shield, the Bay encompasses some of Ontario's most spectacular scenery. It is also one of the province's richest areas for amphibians and reptiles, with 35 species recorded. In Georgian Bay Islands National Park, Beausoleil Island alone, at an area of 1100 ha, supports 32 species. Among the resident herpetofauna are the regionally rare Spotted Turtle, Eastern Hognose Snake, Eastern Fox Snake and Eastern Massasauga. During the summers of 1995 and 1996, herpetofaunal surveys were conducted on 43 of the approximately 30,000 islands in Georgian Bay. This talk will provide an overview of the varied habitats and herpetofauna of this region, as well as a discussion of the biogeographic points of interest.

22081: As consumers of 60-99% of reef primary productivity, herbivorous fishes occupy a pivotal role in channeling energy along the reef food chain. I examined feeding physiology and ecology of two territorial herbivorous damselfishes commonly found among the coral reefs of the San Blas Archipelago, Republic of Panama. I measured gut length, gut retention time, and total and nutrient-specific assimilation efficiencies and made interspecific comparisons between the dusky damselfish (S. dorsopunicans) and the threespot damselfish (S. planifrons). Relative gut length is significantly different between the two damselfish species. Dusky damselfish have a relative gut length ratio (gut length/standard length) of 1.20 and a Zihler index ((gut length/(weight^1/3)) of 3.42. Values for the threespot damselfish are 3.01 and 8.24 respectively. Despite striking differences in RGL and ZI, the gut retention time is the same for both species. Additionally, only protein assimilation efficiency (and thus total assimilation efficiency) varies between species; significantly more protein is assimilated by the threespot damselfish than the dusky damselfish. These results have several important implications. First, as both species feed on the same algal diet, the greater assimilation efficiency of the threespot damselfish may translate into faster growth rates and greater reproductive capacity. Second, it has long been held that relative gut length ratios of herbivorous fishes fall between 2 and 21, with most herbivorous damselfishes in the range of 5. The significantly lower relative gut length of dusky damselfish, unquestionably an herbivore, challenges trophic classifications based on relative gut length ratios. Third, gut morphologies are often used in phylogenetic analyses. These two damselfish are closely related congeners yet their gut morphologies vary significantly. This questions the applicability of such characters in phylogenetic analyses.

22082: Prior to 1991, the sabine shiner, Notropis sabinae, was known only from drainages west of the Mississippi River. 22083: Identification of ichthyoplankton (eggs, larvae, and juveniles) can be a challenging task due to their small sizes and dynamic development. This problem is particularly acute for tropical and subtropical ichthyoplankton, most of which can be identified to family-level only. As part of a broader initiative to develop molecular markers for tropical and subtropical fish identification, we report on the utility of mitochondrial ribosomal gene sequences for triggerfish species identification. A 1,510 bp fragment, containing portions of the mitochondrial ribosomal genes (12S, 16S) and the complete tRNA valine gene, was sequenced from six triggerfish species (4 genera) inhabiting the western central Atlantic Ocean. Forty-three sequences were examined to assess intra- and interspecific variation. Intraspecific differences were minor (less than 0.5%); however, sufficient interspecific differences occur within this locus to allow the design of robust species-specific PCR primers. When tested in a multiplex PCR assay, these primers yielded species-diagnostic size fragments that unambiguously identified all 4 genera and 4 of the 6 species. Distinction between the two Canthidermis congeners (0.9% interspecific variation) was not possible using this approach; however, these congeners were readily distinguished using RFLP analysis of the PCR amplicon. We suggest that molecular genetic approaches can provide a robust and rapid method to tackle long-standing problems in the identification of fish species.

22084: The family Goodeidae is a distinct North American lineage of freshwater fishes and is comprised of two monophyletic subfamilies (Empetrichthyinae and Goodeinae). 22085: Mixing gene pools may cause outbreeding depression (OD). However, it is unknown what kind and degree of between-mate dissimilarity should exist for OD to occur. The Optimum Outbreeding Paradigm (OOP) predicts inbreeding depression (ID) for offspring of close relatives. As similarities between mates decrease, offspring fitness increases, reaches an optimal level and then decreases to levels below parental fitness (i.e., OD occurs). Populations of eastern mosquitofish (Gambusia holbrooki: Poeciliidae) from the Piedmont and Coastal Plain of two drainages were used as sources of fish for seven crosses and six pure controls each replicated in four mesocosms. OD occurred in populations of some crosses between fish from different regions and/or drainages. There were significantly more extinct populations among those founded with fish from the same vs. different region/drainage sections (7 of 20 vs. 3 of 32). Population size and growth rate, fecundity and juvenile survival were significantly lower for populations of crosses of fish from different regions and/or drainages than for those of their controls. I examined potential predictors of OD and the per-locus number of unshared alleles (Nu) between sources was the best predictor under the OOP. Optimum outcrossing and OD are expected when Nu = 0.25 and >0.45, respectively.

22086: Long bones are the major skeletal elements of vertebrate appendages. The radiations of many vertebrate clades were facilitated by locomotory innovations involving these elements (e.g. the terrestrial diversification of tetrapods) and thus it is necessary to understand how these elements changed biomechanically to more fully understand vertebrate evolution. Biomechanical attributes of long bones such as strength, modulus, and loading conditions are well documented in avian and mammalian taxa. However, data for taxa from outgroup clades are virtually non-existent and the results from the few studies that have been conducted are not in accord with those obtained for bird and mammal bones. In order to provide a better understanding of skeletal evolution, I conducted a series of biomechanical tests on long bones from a diversity of fish, amphibians, and reptiles that possessed basal locomotory attributes within their respective clades. Evolutionary trends were assessed using phylogenetic character analysis. The results suggest: 1) material properties (strength, modulus, and failure strain) did not vary throughout evolution, 2) in vivo strain regimes increased independently in birds and mammals, 3) the capacity of long bones to functionally adapt is a plesiomorphic osteichthyan trait, and 4) size and shape changes were the primary means by which long bones changed to meet evolutionary locomotory challenges.

22087: Locomotion in stingrays occurs as waves are propagated along their broadly expanded pectoral fins and can range from being undulatory to oscillatory. This study compares swimming behavior in three stingray species (Taeniura lymma, Dasyatis americana, D. sabina) differing in fin design (disc shape) as measured by aspect ratio (AR). Three-dimensional video recordings captured swimming kinematics over a range of velocities for the three species. Results indicate that D. americana (highest AR) has a significantly lower wing beat frequency and lower number of waves than the other two species. Wing amplitude, as a percentage of wing span, differs significantly in T. lymma (highest) and D. sabina (lowest). The results of frequency and number of waves corroborate previous studies suggesting that higher aspect ratio fins tend to have a lower frequency and lower number of waves than low aspect ratio fins; however, the amplitude data does not fit the prediction of high AR fins having greater amplitude. Overall, D. americana falls more toward the oscillatory end of the continuum and T. lymma falls toward the undulatory end, with D. sabina somewhere in between these two.

22088: The ocular lens of fishes contains mycosporine-like amino acids (MAAs), which attenuate short wavelengths of light. The causes for the varied distribution of MAAs in the lenses of different fish species are still in question. In this study I examined the lenticular MAA content of 42 flatfish species (order Pleuronectiformes) from nine families to investigate the controlling factors on lens pigmentation and changes in pigmentation during ontogeny. MAAs were actively transported and concentrated by the lens from the surrounding humors in the eye. These MAAs produced two absorbance peaks when analyzed spectrophotometrically, one near 320 nm and another near 360 nm. The relative amounts of different MAAs in the lens was correlated with phylogeny, while the total MAA concentration reflected the depth distribution of each species. Species living in deeper water contained lower concentrations of MAAs. Both the total amount of MAAs and their relative proportions changed during ontogeny. MAAs began accumulating after settlement, and increased in concentration with standard length. The phylogenetic trend in the relative proportion of MAA peaks suggests that lens pigmentation is under genetic control. This control is not exerted by the lens itself, but may occur at the level of food metabolism.

22089: Dissolved oxygen (DO) is proving to be one of the most important determinants of juvenile fish growth and survival in our estuaries. Laboratory experiments were conducted to determine the effects of chronic hypoxia and periodic acute hypoxia on the growth, metabolic rate and blood hematocrit of juvenile southern flounder, Paralichthys lethostigma. Fish were maintained in aquaria having constant salinity (15 psu) and temperature (25 °C) and exposed to constant normoxia (6 mg O2 l-1), constant hypoxia (2.75), an intermediate level (4.5), and a diel oscillating treatment (daily mean = 4.5 mg O2 l-1). Results from the blood hematocrit analysis indicate a secondary stress response to the nocturnal hypoxia in the oscillating treatment resulting in increased blood hematocrit levels. Flounder also exhibited limited growth in the low DO treatment (1.9 % Wt d-1, p<0.001) suggesting a species-level limiting oxygen concentration for growth between the low (2.75) and intermediate (4.5) DO levels. Furthermore, fish in the oscillating treatment realized growth similar to the intermediate treatment indicating that daily growth is a function of the daily mean DO concentrations. This hypothesis is supported by the dramatic overcompensation in the afternoon routine respiration rates exhibited by the oscillating treatment. Further work is necessary to address the synergistic effects of temperature and variable DO on the growth and physiology of juvenile estuarine dependent fish.

22091: Distributional patterns of species result in part from their ability to tolerate physiologically the environmental extremes characteristic within their geographical range. Macroecology attempts to reveal relationships between organisms and their environments by investigating statistical patterns of abundance and distribution. In such analyses, species serve as replicates where the relationship between range and body size is used to understand how physical space and ecological resources are partitioned to create the unique distributions of species. However, these studies often fail to consider the underlying physiological capacities and tolerances that are most likely to be the limiting factors in determining distributions. I measured temperature dependent metabolic rate and high temperature tolerance in several ectothermic species in an attempt to investigate two subsidiary principles of Shelford's law and determine if physiological parameters are better predictors of distributional patterns than are measures of body size. After controls for phylogeny, I found species-specific plasticity of metabolic rate and high temperature tolerance to predict better the statistical patterns of geographic range size and latitudinal range among the fishes and snakes studied. These findings support Shelford's idea that the distributions of species often are governed by the environmental factor for which species have the narrowest tolerance range or least adaptability.

22092: Substantial individual variation in timing of emergence from hibernation has been reported among reptiles, although few studies have addressed the causes of that variation. Here we report patterns of spring emergence by black rat snakes (Elaphe obsoleta obsoleta), observed at 13 communal hibernacula in eastern Ontario from 1992 to 1997. Although we found significant variations in timing of emergence among years and among hibernacula, we found no evidence of a simple latitudinal gradient in mean emergence dates. Within hibernacula, significantly more snakes emerged on days with high maximum air temperatures, but maximum air temperature only explained a small amount of the variation among years in emergence dates. Larger individuals emerged earlier than smaller individuals and females tended to emerge earlier than males. Condition was not a significant factor determining timing of emergence in our black rat snake population. Based on these results, we proposed the preparation for reproduction hypothesis which states that mature individual snakes emerge earlier than immature individuals to prepare their gonads for reproduction.

22093: The Brown Tree Snake (BTS), Boiga irregularis, is a nocturnal, arboreal species accidentally introduced to the island of Guam, and associated with the loss of most of the island's native forest vertebrates. Little is known about the movement patterns of this species or that of other nocturnal, arboreal snakes. I investigated the overnight spatial movement patterns of BTS using two tracking devices; standard radio telemetry and a quilting cocoon of cotton thread (240 m), which delineated the snake's path. I recorded microhabitat data at every one meter interval along the tracking thread path. Ten BTS were tracked a minimum of 30 meters (mean = 92.9 m). The total distances moved were on average twice the straight-line distance from initial capture/release location to refugium. There was no significant correlation between body size and percentage of movement above ground, mean height above ground, or mean height of forest canopy used. There was a significant positive relationship between mean support diameter and BTS body size (R square = 0.596, P = 0.0148). There was also a significant positive relationship between available forest connectivity and snake pathways. Snakes used certain plants in disproportion to their occurrence in the forest according to relative stability or degree of connectivity.

22094: Studies on box turtles (Terrapene carolina baurii) on Egmont Key have been ongoing since 1991. This island off the west coast of Florida is home to more than 2000 turtles. During previous fieldwork, large numbers of juveniles were found. Data on size, habitat, and activity were recorded. Thread trailers were attached to 59 juveniles (<121mm) that were tracked until the thread ran out (generally within four days). I recorded canopy cover density and species composition along trails at 10m intervals. Juveniles were found primarily under dense, low ground cover, and frequently travelled at the ecotone between dense canopy and more open areas. 22095: The diamondback terrapin, Malaclemys terrapin, is the only species of estuarine turtle. The range of Malaclemys extends along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts from Cape Cod to Corpus Christi. 22096: Populations of the yellow-blotched map turtle (Graptemys flavimaculata) are known to be declining throughout their limited range. 22097: I experimentally tested innate prey preference in brown water snakes, Nerodia taxispilota. Nerodia taxispilota is a piscivorous species, and adults consume primarily catfishes (Ictaluridae). 22098: Recent work on a variety of reptiles provides strong evidence that incubation temperatures can influence many aspects of a hatchling's phenotype (i.e., size, shape, activity, locomotor performance, etc.). However, although these traits seem likely to affect the hatchling's fitness, few studies have tested this assumption. Vulnerability to predation is one plausible way that phenotypic modifications could affect an organism's fitness. Therefore, we incubated the eggs of lizards at temperatures similar to the extremes of natural nests, and examined both the response of hatchlings to predator (snake) scent and actual vulnerability in staged encounters in the laboratory. We used two species of montane Australian scincids: one heliotherm (Lampropholis delicata) that deposits eggs in relatively warm nests, and one thigmotherm (Nannoscincus maccoyi) that lays in relatively cool nests. For both species, our results show that incubation temperature affects both an individual's response to predator scent and its vulnerability to predation. These patterns are complex, and change with the age of the hatchling, perhaps through differential growth rates and changes in activity patterns. Nevertheless, these experiments support the notion that incubation-induced modifications to a lizard's phenotype may be biologically significant, and that some of these effects are mediated through predator-prey interactions.

22099: Since 1995, we have been studying the only known population of gopher frogs (Rana capito) in Mississippi to investigate variation in reproductive traits and population demography. Adult size structure, adult survivorship, reproductive success, and juvenile recruitment were monitored through the combination of a complete drift fence and egg mass surveys. We found no repeatability among years in the relationship between the number of females, egg masses, and emerging juveniles. These data suggest that monitoring through the exclusive use of either egg mass surveys or drift fences may not accurately determine the status of anuran populations. 22100: Whiptail lizards of the species genus Cnemidophorus range across the southwestern U.S. into South America. They occupy a variety of habitats and, although they vary in behaviour and ecology, are morphologically conservative. At some point in their evolutionary history, different combinations of species have hybridized to form all-female, self-cloning species. Using information from allozymes, skull morphology, and mitochondrial DNA sequences genes, I am sorting out the evolutionary relationships among North American species of Cnemidophorus to determine: (a) how closely related species have to be to form viable, hybrid unisexuals; (b) whether morphological and ecological similarities among the various species result from common descent or adaptation to similar environments; (c) how and when these lizards speciated and got to where we find them today. Results to date suggest that some of the incredible speciation in Cnemidophorus is due to rapid fragmentation and isolation during the Late Pleistocene, but that some speciation events may have occurred much earlier. 22101: We used data from 88 litters of northern water snakes (Nerodia sipedon) to test predictions about how mothers should adaptively vary the sex ratios of their offspring. Sex ratios did not vary with birth date, but larger mothers produced significantly more daughters, and mothers producing larger offspring produced significantly more daughters. Because neonate size did vary with maternal size, the two significant sex ratio patterns were independent of each other. The limited evidence on neonatal sex ratios for other snake species also indicates variation that is non-random but not necessarily adaptive. Better understanding of these patterns will require information on the factors that differentially affect the fitness of male and female neonates.

22102: We examined the reproductive ecology and natural history of Rana pipiens in a recently rehabilitated wetland in Barberton, Ohio during the spring and summers of 1996 and 1997. 22103: Surveys of calling amphibians in marshes located in Ontario and the Great Lakes' states were conducted by volunteers from April to July in 1995 through the Marsh Monitoring Program. 22104: Plot sampling was used to compare the wet and dry season litter herpetofaunas of three forest types in Kibale National Park, Uganda. 22105: Throughout the tropics, mature forests are rapidly being replaced with pastures, gardens, and plantations. 22106: This study was performed to establish a mean cardiac and respiration rate in juvenile southern stingrays (Dasyatis americana). 22107: Harvesting of Alberta's boreal forest is increasing dramatically. Predicted effects of forest harvesting on lakes in this region involve increases in nutrient loading and primary productivity. 22109: The short-term, localized nature of grouper spawning aggregations and unequal sex ratios due to protogyny renders many groupers particularly vulnerable to fishing pressure and therefore in need of special management techniques. 22114: Aquatic organisms must maintain an optimal buoyancy to minimize energy expended in locomotion and holding vertical position in the water column. 22117: Research was conducted in the North Fork of the Virgin River within Zion National Park, Utah, USA, to investigate the effects of chronic recreational disturbance on the native fish community. 22132: We studied mating behavior and reproductive success in a wild, northern population of bullfrogs (Rana catesbeiana). The predominant selective mechanism in this system was female choice. Male bullfrogs gathered annually at traditional chorusing sites where they competed aggressively or employed alternate mating strategies in an attempt to acquire mates. Females entered the choruses briefly to select a mate, engage in amplexus, and deposit eggs. Compared with males that were unsuccessful in obtaining mates, reproductively successful males were larger, had longer tenures in the choruses, spent more of their tenure calling, and had previous chorusing experience. Male size was related to reproductive effort with larger males losing proportionately more weight over the chorusing season. In females, clutch volume was positively related to body size with large females depositing egg masses up to three times larger than those of small females. There was no evidence of assortative mating by body size. We also postulated that, because of a low population density, this system may best be described as a lek in contrast to the resource-defense system described previously for this species.

22133: I conducted field studies to determine the influence of female Dendrobates pumilio on offspring survival through two forms of maternal care; rearing site selection and nutritional provisioning. Female D. pumilio transport tadpoles from hatching sites to water-filled leaf axils where they are tended until metamorphosis. I assessed availability and variability of rearing axils (pH, temperature, water volume, height, cover), female choice of rearing sites, and effects of site characters on tadpole survival. Rearing sites are abundant and highly variable. While female choice is best predicted by a combination of low height and pH, tadpole survival is best predicted by variance in axil temperature. These results suggest that although females deposit their tadpoles non-randomly, rearing site selection does not influence tadpole fitness. Females return to tadpole rearing sites to provide eggs for their tadpoles to eat throughout development. I observed females tending tadpoles to determine the influence of provisioning on tadpole fitness. Provisioning behaviors such as time to first feeding, frequency of feedings, and number of eggs per feeding are highly variable. Although there is substantial variation in provisioning, preliminary analyses indicate that predation [text partly illegible] provisioning on tadpole survival, limiting the potential for further evolution of provisioning.

22134: Iteroparous animals that have substantial investment in parental care should invest energy differentially into growth and reproduction according to size and age. Smaller, younger animals should invest more energy in growth for future reproductive benefits, while larger, older animals should invest more energy in reproduction and parental care. In this study, 22 gravid female red-backed salamanders (Plethodon cinereus) were induced to oviposit in the laboratory, and brooding behavior was recorded for salamanders with body sizes ranging from 34 mm to 53 mm SVL. Female body size was positively correlated with clutch size. Females that oviposited atypically and/or terminated parental care by oophagy were significantly smaller than females who reared their clutches normally. These results suggest that smaller females may forego reproduction to invest in growth, while larger females should always invest in reproduction.

22135: Males of the hylid Smilisca phaeota have complex advertisement calls which show a large amount of variation in several frequency related traits. Two of these traits were found to be negatively correlated with each other in the natural population studied. Female preferences for male calls were tested in and around the correlation of these two traits. Initial results demonstrated that females have directional preferences for both traits when measured independently. Females were found to have preferences which exert a stabilizing effect on the correlation in the two trait space. As a result of these preferences, the directionality of preference for any one trait taken independently can change depending on the relation of that trait to a second trait.
Dept. of Zoology, University of Texas, Austin, TX 78712, USA
22136: The reproductive behaviors of a bromeliad-breeding tree frog, Osteocephalus planiceps (Hylidae) were studied in Amazonian Peru. Pairs of this species form where males defend oviposition territories (i.e. bromeliads), and females return periodically to amplex with the males to lay fertilized trophic eggs for their developing tadpoles. To determine the extent of biparental care and how biparental care and resource defense affect the mating system, I relocated bromeliads within a 1-ha study area into clumped versus isolated oviposition sites. In addition, 12 artificial bromeliads were provided so that egg deposition and tadpole survival could be monitored at those sites. All matings in the study site were recorded for a five-month period, and the number of metamorphs produced in the artificial bromeliads was used to evaluate individual reproductive success. Although males and females form monogamous pairs due to site-fidelity, several ecological factors seem to maintain a rather fluid mating system. Limited oviposition sites, relative proximity of oviposition sites (one male's territory may include more than one oviposition site and, therefore, can potentially accommodate more than one female), and high predation pressure all contribute to continuous changes in the mating system.

22137: Females of the hylid Smilisca phaeota were found to have significantly different preferences for male advertisment calls under different simulated chorusing behaviors. Male Smilisca phaeota often try to overlap their calls with those of another male. This behavior is common but not ubiquitous. Females presented with a pair of test calls given in an overlapping sequence that was controlled for lead calling. Females preference was found to be significant and opposite that of females given the same pair of test calls in an alternating sequence. Male chorusing behavior was found to reflect the apparent diversifying selection from female preferences. Male-male interactions were recorded in the field using males of noticably different call types. Males which had a lower dominant frequency correspond to the male type chosen by females when test calls were given alternately. Males with a higher dominant frequency correspond with the test calls that were chosen by females in the overlapping test. Interactions of male-male pairs in the field have shown that males behave in a way that would be expected by the female choice.

22138: Sexual selection and mating system theories predict that individuals will be more selective the higher the mating investment they make. Hence, animals that do not make a high reproductive investment will increase their fitness by increasing number of matings, while animals that have a high investment per mating will be "choosy". While studying the mating system of the anaconda, we opportunistically collected 45 breeding aggregations for six years. Females lie apparently passive in shallow water while the males coil around her (males number from 1 to 17, with a mean of 3.8). No fights or ritualized displays were seen among the males. Each female is attractive to males for about four weeks throughout the breeding season, which lasts from mid-February to mid-May. Longer males were found with heavier females (r= 0.48; p= 0.008) and the latter were courted by a greater number of males (r= 0.44; p= 0.02). This suggests that males prefer to court females with higher fecundity and breeding status, since random mating would not produce this tendencies. Due to the short time that the breeding season lasts (in respect to the duration of the breeding ball), and the fact that receptive females are not clumped together, it is unlikely that one male can find many females in one season. Although a lot remains to be studied, it appears that the mating system of the anacondas is polyandric; where males select the more fecund females.

22139: Common death adders (Elapidae) from Australia have convergent reproductive and dietary adaptations with vipers. They reproduce biannually, show ontogenetic shifts from endothermic to ectothermic prey, and are ambush predators. I examined 208 Acanthophis antarcticus from the collections of the California Academy of Sciences. Morphometric data, sex, age, seasonal reproductive status, size of eggs or follicles, and stomach and hindgut contents were determined. Preliminary results suggest that approximately 30% of snakes had hindgut or stomach contents. Some examples of hindgut and stomach contents included lizard eggs, insect legs, a skink jaw, unidentified bone fragments, and possibly fur. Therefore these death adders appear to prey mostly on ectotherms. Sizes of adult Australian Acanthophis antarcticus from previous studies were on average 30% larger than the Papua New Guinea specimens examined. Initial results show that the majority of females from Papua New Guinea were gravid in December, implying annual reproductivity. Thus these smaller snakes are not displaying convergent ecological characteristics with vipers like their Australian counterparts.

22140: Crotaphytid lizards exhibit a morphological trend in several musculo-skeletal characteristics of the trophic apparatus that are correlated with ecological and behavioral attributes, particularly concerning saurophagy and durophagy. Quantification of bite-force performance of taxa representing the primary crotaphytid morphotypes, with respect to trophic apparatus structure, provides performance parameters that relate trophic apparatus structure to dietary ecology and feeding behavior. Data on trophic apparatus musculo-skeletal structure, bite-force performance, feeding behavior, and dietary ecology permit the generation of testable predictions of ecomorphological relationships for other crotaphytid taxa. Examination of crotaphytid feeding biology within a comparative phylogenetic framework reveals that crotaphytids exhibit concordant evolution among trophic apparatus morphology and performance, dietary ecology, and feeding behavior. In addition, increased saurophagy, together with correlated specializations at several levels, appears to have evolved convergently within the Crotaphytidae.

22141: Previous analyses indicated that American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis) population densities in 60 Florida lakes were significantly correlated with parameters historically used to evaluate system trophic state (total phosphorus, total nitrogen, water column chlorophyll a, and water transparency). Recent examination of these and other data have begun to reveal some interesting patterns regarding environmental factors and the abundance of this crocodilian. Alligator density was uncorrelated with limnetic zone fish biomass and only slightly correlated with littoral zone fish biomass, but was strongly correlated with whole-lake fish biomass (r2 = 0.45, p < 0.0001). Other environmental factors which were found to covary with alligator population size were lake color (r2 = 0.37, p < 0.0001) and macrophyte coverage (r2 = 0.28, p = 0.0015); those which were inversely related were mean lake depth (r2 = 0.49, p < 0.0001) and percentage of human-developed shoreline (r2 = 0.38, p < 0.0001). Finally, while as much as 55% of the variation in alligator population densities among lakes could be accounted for by total phosphorus (p < 0.0001), multiple linear regressions using other parameters (plant coverage, water transparency, and fish biomass) could account for up to 78% of the variation in abundance (p < 0.0001). These models are discussed with respect to ecological processes present in lakes and their usefulness to game managers and to scientists who attempt to detect human impacts on populations.

22142: Animal dispersion patterns are influenced by the distribution and abundance of resources and other individuals, both of which are features of the local environment. A previous study indicates that moisture determines the extent to which food and mates are limited for red-backed salamanders (Plethodon cinereus), so predictable differences in moisture levels between populations may result in different dispersion patterns. I monitored shelter use and cohabitation at two sites (wetter vs. drier) using mark-recapture to determine whether shelter fidelity and incidence of cohabitation differ between sites. Both males and females at the wetter site demonstrated lower fidelity, but only females at the wetter site exhibited greater incidence of intrasexual cohabitation. Wetter site males showed low occurrences of intrasexual cohabitation, as did drier site males and females. These results indicate that salamanders in wetter habitats may not hold fixed territories, probably in response to increased food availability. Low fidelity and low intrasexual cohabitation by wetter site males may indicate the existence of ephemeral mating territories. Differences in spacing patterns in response to local environmental conditions may have important repercussions for salamander population dynamics and sexual selection.

22143: The United States has approximately 55 x 10^5 km of rivers. From this total only 1.9% are considered worthy of Federal protection (< 100,000 km), due primarily to human induced changes on the landscape. The Ohio River exhibits anthropogenic scars, as do the embayments associated with the river. Between Parkersburg, WV and Cincinnati, OH I sampled six embayments with different geomorphology, upstream landuse, and habitat conditions. Fishes were collected from these habitats using both gill nets and electrofishing equipment from April through October 1997. I examined habitat use patterns over different spatial scales and found variable patterns in both micro- and macro-scale habitat use. For example, sunfish (Lepomis sp.) used near shore areas in all embayments. Gizzard shad (Dorosoma cepedianum) were collected everywhere in shallow embayments and only in open water areas in deep embayments. On a landscape level fish densities changed as a result of up- mid- or downstream location within an embayment. Integrating information on landuse, physical characteristics, and fish assemblages over different spatial and temporal scales will result in a more complete understanding of the factors influencing these patterns. This information has the potential to inspire better conservation and restoration efforts for these unique habitats along the Ohio River.

22144: Predator inspection behavior was investigated in three sympatric species of coral reef fish that differed in body morphology, and in two habitats that differed in structural complexity. It was hypothesized that the deep-bodied species would exhibit the riskiest behavior during predator inspections due to their protection from gape-limited predators, and that the shallow-bodied species would be risk-averse. It was also expected that the riskiest inspection behavior would occur in the most complex habitat, due to the presence of prey refuges. Bluehead wrasse, the species most at risk due to the slender body morphology, inspected the predator at greater distances than the other species (ocean surgeonfish, foureye butterflyfish). The percentage of inspections tended to increase with increased body depth across species, indicating risk-averse behavior by the wrasse. Inspection distances decreased in complex habitats for wrasse and surgeonfish, but not butterflyfish, the species with the greatest body depth. Similarly, the percentage of inspections tended to increase in the complex habitat for wrasse and surgeonfish, but not butterflyfish. These data suggest that individuals assessed their overall predation risk related to body morphology and adjusted their inspection behavior, whereas habitat complexity differences played a minor role in predator inspection behavior.

22145: Although lakes are often inter-connected waterbodies, few studies have examined isolation among lakes as a determinant of fish species diversity and/or community composition. In this study I examine the fish species composition and spatial arrangement of 52 lakes located within two south-central Ontario watersheds, and assess the degree of spatial isolation between lakes. Measures of lake isolation incorporated watercourse distance, lake elevation, upstream watercourse distance, and waterbodies as fish "stepping stones". Many of these isolation measures were based on ecological considerations, i.e. the "challenges" a fish faces in moving between lakes, as compared to the straight-line distance between sampling locations which is often used in studies of this nature. Eight isolation measures were examined for their degree of association with patterns in fish species composition. The results indicated that conventional straight-line distance between lakes does not accurately portray the degree of isolation. This study illustrates the importance of examining alternative measures of lake isolation when exploring patterns in fish species distributions, since the isolation of waterbodies increase the rate of local extinction. Therefore, interconnected lakes could potentially provide a "rescue effect" for lakes with threatened aquatic fauna.

22146: Factors that affect growth rate (e.g. food supply) should affect juvenile survival and thus year-class strength since the principle sources of mortality for young fish-predation and starvation-are size dependent. In 1996, experimental ponds (area=360 m2/pond) were used to study the effects of nutrient addition on production, growth and survival of age-0 fathead minnows. Each pond was divided in half; one side was treated regularly with inorganic fertilizers (P, N) to maintain nutrient concentrations at levels three times higher than control sides. Chl a was measured to be 7 fold greater in treated versus untreated pond sides. Number of eggs hatched and end-of-season age-0 fish survival and sizes were also greater in the treated pond sides. We analyzed otolith microstructure to investigate the mechanisms behind the observed contrasts in age-0 lengths and survival in the different nutrient regimes. Hatching distributions and back-calculated age-0 fish lengths were compared with those observed throughout the season. Surprisingly, preliminary results suggest age-0 fish survival was not directly influenced by size-selective mortality. Instead, treatment survivors hatched over the entire spawning season; control survivors hatched primarily in the second half of the spawning season. These results suggest that conditions during early periods of growth can influence lengths and survival of age-0 fish. Since over-winter mortality (examined during a 1995-96 experiment) was found to be strongly size-selective, it follows that mechanisms acting in the first few weeks after hatching can ultimately affect the number of fish recruited to the next spawning season.

22147: The life history of the flagfin shiner, Pteronotropis signipinnis, was described from a population occurring in a second-order blackwater stream in southeast Mississippi. Analysis of length frequency histograms indicated a life span of one to two years. Females were reproductive from April to mid-August. Sex ratio was not significantly different from a 1:1 ratio. Adult males were larger and more heavily pigmented near the abdomen than females. All females reached sexual maturity by 27 mm SL and produced multiple clutches of ova. Clutch size ranged from 12 to 101 ova and was significantly correlated with SL. Mean mature oocyte diameter was 0.88 mm (range 0.76 to 0.96).
Department of Biological Sciences, The University of Southern Mississippi, Hattiesburg, MS 39406-5018
22148: Freshwater populations of threespine stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) exhibit a tremendous amount of adaptive variation in a number of traits. One classic example is male nuptial colouration in populations from the Chehalis River drainage basin in Washington State. Males in these populations assume a jet-black nuptial colouration, rather than the red underside and blue-green dorsum that is typical of the species. A widely cited, yet poorly tested, hypothesis to account for the evolution of the black nuptial colouration in these populations is the threat display convergence hypothesis. The hypothesis contends that the black nuptial colouration evolved in response to competition for nesting territories with the co-distributed Olympic mudminnow (Novumbra hubbsi), which is also black, territorial for nest sites and breeds at the same time of year as stickleback. The hypothesis produces the prediction that mudminnows have a greater impact on the reproductive success of typical, red male sticklebacks than on that of black male sticklebacks. I tested this prediction by manipulating the presence/absence of mudminnows and the colour type of stickleback present in screened exclosures in several wetland areas (typical nesting habitat for both species). Also, I conducted several field surveys of nesting sticklebacks to determine (i) the frequency and outcome of interactions between nesting sticklebacks and mudminnows and (ii) the temporal development of black nuptial coloration.
Biology, Clark University, Worcester, MA 01610, USA
22149: Liolaemus is a large genus of lizards in the family Iguanidae with greater than 160 species distributed throughout the southern half of South America on either side of the Andes. Relationships among Liolaemus species remain unresolved. Approximately 1800 bases of aligned mitochondrial DNA sequence data were obtained from regions encoding the ND1, ND2, COI, and eight transfer RNA genes. A phylogenetic hypothesis is generated for 55 ingroup species and four outgroup species. Four alternative biogeographic hypotheses are suggested for the early diversification of Liolaemus. The most parsimonious tree is highly suggestive of an east-west vicariant split due to the uplift of the Andes at least 10-15 million years ago.

22150: We surveyed mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequence variation in the sagebrush lizard (Sceloporus graciosus) from throughout California, as well as populations from Oregon, Utah, New Mexico, and Baja California, including all three currently recognized subspecies. We used these data to estimate the intraspecific phylogeny and to develop a biogeographic scenario to account for the geographic structure of this species. We sequenced ~900 bp of the mtDNA ND4 gene and adjacent tRNAs from 26 populations of S. graciosus (including S. arenicolus) and five putative outgroups (S. scalaris, S. jarrovii, S. clarkii, S. occidentalis, and S. variabilis). The phylogenetic hypotheses best supported by the data do not support the currently recognized subspecies as evolutionary units. The present distribution of S. graciosus in California is represented by four distinct clades: southern Great Basin (including S. arenicolus), eastern + southwestern Sierra, northern California + Coast Ranges, and Peninsular Ranges. A scenario for the historic biogeography of S. graciosus is consistent with current views of the geologic and climatic changes in California during the past 20 million years.

22151: Among archaeobatrachians, the largest and most poorly known group is the Pelobatoidea. Within this group, the morphology and relationships of frogs in the genera Pelobates, Scaphiopus, and Spea remain poorly understood. I compared the osteology of these taxa using cleared and double-stained and dry-skeletal preparations. Spea and Scaphiopus share several morphologies, including absence of quadratojugals, presence of palatine processes of the facial processes of the maxillae, long vomerine postchoanal processes, and completely cartilaginous sternums. Spea is characterized by poorly developed maxillary processes of the nasals and the lack of well-developed posteromedial processes of the parasphenoid. I reassessed the phylogenetic relationships of these frogs using osteological characters sampled from all recognized taxa of Pelobates, Scaphiopus, and Spea, and one species each of Megophrys, Leptobrachium, Pelodytes, Rhinophrynus, Xenopus, Limnodynastes, and Discoglossus as outgroup taxa. Preliminary results support Pelobates as the sister group to Scaphiopus. This may be an artifact of convergences in skull morphology relating to the degree of hyperossification of these taxa or may indicate an evolutionary history of these frogs that disagrees with the currently accepted phylogeny.

22152: Anurans inhabiting northern locales survive the winter by avoiding cold through aquatic hibernation or burrowing, or by tolerating freezing of their tissues. This study describes the overwintering strategy of the most aquatic of the North American hylids, the northern cricket frog (Acris crepitans). Laboratory choice tests indicated that cricket frogs choose terrestrial hibernacula, especially under leaf litter in shallow depressions, when faced with decreasing temperatures. However, unlike Bufo and some Pseudacris, cricket frogs did not burrow when air temperatures dropped, even when faced with desiccating conditions. Surprisingly, cricket frogs are not freeze tolerant like most other nearctic hylids that hibernate in terrestrial sites. Given these data, field searches were conducted and cricket frogs were found hibernating in crayfish burrows and other cavities along the pond's edge - sites which provide full protection from freezing. In conclusion, cricket frogs can neither burrow nor survive freezing, and therefore require pre-existing subterranean sites to successfully overwinter. Thus, I suggest that habitat quality and winter severity be explored as possible causes of this species' decline in the northern portion of its range.

22153: The nine species of Peltophryne are endemic to the islands of the Caribbean, ranging from Cuba to the Virgin Islands. Pregill (1981) presented three synapomorphies to support the monophyly of Peltophryne (with the exception of P. fluviatica): the maxillae extend anteriorly to meet in front of the premaxillae; the zygomatic ramus of the squamosal extends ventrally to abut the maxilla; and the zygomatic and ventral rami of the squamosal are connected by a flange. These characters are redescribed and their phylogenetic utility is discussed; in particular, the "rostral" element is reinterpreted and presented as support for the monophyly of the entire group. Based on cranial morphology and geographic proximity, Bufo granulosus has been proposed as the sister taxon to Peltophryne; comparisons of the morphology of the these taxa are made. A preliminary analysis of the phylogenetic relationships of the nine species of Peltophryne was conducted using characters from osteology and external morphology; the results of this analysis are presented.

22154: The purpose of this investigation was to identify differences in resource allocation strategies between freshwater and brackish water populations of the Northern Water Snake, Nerodia sipedon. We also sought evidence that populations of the Northern Water Snake are adapting to estuarine environments. Gravid females were collected from two brackish and two freshwater sites. The snakes' reproductive outputs were estimated using relative clutch mass, adjusted for female condition. Neonates from each environment were raised in both freshwater and 25% sea water to determine the environmental effects on growth, metabolism, and survival. Freshwater snakes allocated 40% more energy to reproduction than estuarine snakes. The growth rates of both groups were reduced in 25% sea water. However, the freshwater neonates raised in 25% sea water became bloated and suffered 40% mortality. The metabolic rates of estuarine snakes was significantly higher in both environments. The results indicate that freshwater snakes allocate a greater proportion of their energy to growth and reproduction, while estuarine snakes incur a higher maintenance cost. Sufficient physiological and behavioral differentiation has occurred between these ecologically distinct populations such that freshwater snakes suffer a substantially reduced fitness in estuarine environments.

22155: Although models for gape cycle evolution in primitive tetrapods have been proposed, little data exists on the feeding kinematics in lizards. Of those studies published in this area, very few have described prey ingestion in scleroglossan lizards. The goal of the present study is to investigate feeding kinematics in the rainbow whiptail (Cnemidophorus lemniscatus; Teiidae) in relation to existing models of prey ingestion in primitive tetrapods. Feeding behavior in the rainbow whiptail was studied using high-speed video with gape cycle kinematics quantified by the construction of kinematic profiles from digitized landmark data of lizards ingesting crickets. In all feeding bouts observed, C. lemniscatus used oral prehension as the sole means of prey capture. During prey ingestion, the tongue is used extensively to manipulate and swallow prey items. Patterns of gape kinematics in this species will be discussed in light of existing models of kinematic evolution and used to refine current ideas and questions regarding prey ingestion in lizards.

22156: A population of striped newts was monitored during three consecutive years to determine patterns of paedomorphosis and metamorphosis. The study site, One Shot Pond, is a temporary pond located on the Katharine Ordway Preserve-Carl Swisher Memorial Sanctuary, Putnam Co., Florida. Newts were sampled monthly via dip net throughout the study period and a continuous drift fence was erected around the pond during the second half of the study period. In the first year, very few newts underwent metamorphosis; the vast majority of larvae appeared to mature and breed as paedomorphs. Few aquatic adults contributed to reproductive output in year one. In contrast, the year two cohort was characterized by a large percentage of metamorphosis as well as paedomorphosis. Over 1,200 newts left the pond as efts in the fall of year two. Like year one though, few aquatic adults contributed to reproductive output in year two. In years one and two, paedomorphic individuals underwent metamorphosis during the following Spring/Summer. Very few larvae were encountered in year three. As a result, relatively few efts emigrated in the fall of year three. However, there was a large immigration of individuals (>2,000) from the surrounding uplands. Although paedomorphosis occurred, the vast majority of reproductive newts were aquatic adults in year three.

22157: Physical aspects of the maternal phenotype are recently recognized as important covariates of the nature of reproduction (ie size vs. number of eggs). We document variation in reproductive phenology, total clutch mass, clutch size and egg mass among seasons and years within a natural population of Galapagos lava lizards (Microlophus (=Tropidurus) delanonis). Maternal size correlates with total clutch mass, clutch size, and egg mass but does not affect the pattern of variation in these traits among time periods. We estimated maternal condition (a measure of energy reserve) and found that it has a significant, positive relationship with each component of reproduction. However, the differences among time periods remained after controlling for this factor. We did not find the expected negative relationship between clutch size and egg mass after controlling for both maternal size and condition. All variables were positively correlated with rain that fell one month prior to oviposition. While maternal characteristics explain some seasonal and annual variation in components of reproduction, we propose that remaining temporal variation may be a response to differences between seasons in direct selection on eggs and/or hatchlings.

22158: In many birds, clutch size is positively correlated with breeding date. Price et al. (1988) presented a model that suggested this is due to differences in female nutritional condition. A similar phenomena occurs in S. miliarius. We collected data on parturition date and litter size for 153 gravid females collected over a six-year period in central Florida. There are consistently strong correlations between total litter mass or litter size and parturition date in these snakes. Annual variation in mean parturition date appears to be driven by annual variation in clutch mass, not in annual variation in climatic conditions. The correlation between parturition date and litter size is not due to enhanced thermoregulatory abilities for larger snakes since snake size is only weakly correlated to parturition date. The relationship between litter mass and parturition date also occurs in several other species of snakes. Ironically, the model developed by Price et al. appears to work better for snakes and other capital breeders than it does for birds and other investment breeders.

22159: Little is known about seasonal patterns in the reproductive phenology of many species of tropical reptiles. Several researchers have demonstrated how reproductive patterns are related to seasonal and annual cycles. Studies of the reproduction of tropical lizards have suggested that wet and dry seasons play a role in the timing of reproduction and recruitment of species. Lizard specimens collected from Costa Rica over a two-year period have been examined for reproductive condition. This collection offers an ideal data set for the study of reproductive patterns in a diverse group of Neotropical leaf-litter lizards. Gonad length in males and the number and length of oviductal eggs in females were recorded. Spatial and temporal analysis of these data provides information on the reproductive phenology. Results will be presented for several species of lizards including Sphenomorphus cherriei and Norops limifrons.

22160: The reproductive cycle is described for females and males of Urosaurus bicarinatus studied from 1988 to 1990 near Chamela, Jalisco, Mexico. Males reached sexual maturity at 38.0 mm snout-vent length (SVL) at an age 8 mo, while females reached sexual maturity at 40.0 mm SVL at an age of 9 mo. Testes of adult males began to increase in size in early April, maximal testes mass occurred in June-August, and testes began to decrease in size, reaching minimum size in October. 22164: The spatial distribution and timing of sexual receptivity of female snakes are important determinants of snake mating systems. 22166: Rapid embryonic development is a potential adaptation to cold climates. 22167: Determinants of embryonic stage at oviposition in the oviparous lizard, Urosaurus ornatus were investigated to gain insight into the reason(s) that most squamate reptiles oviposit when embryos reach stage 30. 22171: Zelditch and Fink have argued that the method of thin-plate splines decomposed by its partial warps can yield phylogenetically informative characters, which can be subjected to the same tests of homology and character independence as are applied to conventional morphological characters. 22172: In fishes, only two distantly related groups of suckermouth armored catfishes (Loricariidae) are known to eat wood: Panaque and the Hypostomus cochliodon species group. 22188: Winter's freezing temperatures exert a major selective force on temperate frogs and toads. 22194: Passive (gliding) flight has been studied in some vertebrate fliers, but is essentially unexplored in the flying snakes of the genus Chrysopelea. 22210: The corn snake, northern pine snake, and eastern king snake reach the northern limit of their range in the Pine Barrens of southern New Jersey. The timber rattlesnake and northern black racer are within the eastern core of their range in the Pine Barrens. These species have developed different strategies to cope with harsh winter temperatures. Radio-telemetry was used to locate hibernacula. Drift fences were used to determine dates of emergence and ingress for 113 pine snakes (6 dens), 66 black racers (5 dens), 61 corn snakes (6 dens), and 4 king snakes (1 den). Physical characteristics of the underground den structure and the depth at which the snakes hibernated was observed by excavating 3 timber rattlesnakes (2 dens), 1 king snake (1 den), 12 corn snakes (3 dens), 196 pine snakes (8 dens), and 41 black racers (6 dens). Rattlesnakes (N=45) and king snakes (N=6) were observed to hibernate in shallow, water-filled cavities and tunnels along the edge of stream corridors. The snakes were found beneath the roots of Atlantic white cedar, black gum, or red maple trees and Sphagnum mats, at an average depth of 30 cm, and were partially submerged in water. Corn snakes, pine snakes, and black racers often share the same upland hibernacula, which are generally located in stump holes or abandoned mammal burrows at an average depth of 1.0 meter. The earliest dates for emergence and latest dates for ingress to dens are: pine snake emergence = March 25, return = November 27; corn snake emergence = March 14, return = November 16; black racer emergence = March 20, return = November 11; timber rattlesnake emergence = April 20.

22211: Painted turtles (Chrysemys picta) hatch in late summer but usually remain in the nest during winter. Hatchlings can survive subzero temperatures in the nest either by tolerating the freezing of their body tissues, at temperatures to -4 °C, or by avoiding ice nucleation and remaining supercooled (unfrozen) to temperatures at least as low as -12 °C. We investigated the effects of soil composition and soil moisture on susceptibility to ice inoculation in hatchling turtles endemic to the sandhills of Nebraska, where soil moisture in winter is variable (range 4-14%). Turtles cooled in frozen, native soil (predominantly sand) froze at -1.6 °C, whereas turtles cooled in frozen soil to which clay or peat was added supercooled to -13 °C before freezing. Avoidance of inoculation by environmental ice in turtles exposed to frozen native soil was possible only when the soil contained little moisture (<4%). Thus, survival of relatively low nest temperatures, by supercooling, may be greater for turtles hibernating in sandy soils containing little moisture, or in soils containing clay or organic matter. However, the winter microenvironment contains numerous ice nuclei (e.g., inorganic particulates, microorganisms) that may nevertheless promote inoculative freezing.

22212: Although studies of body temperature (Tb) are extensive for snakes living in temperate regions, few studies have focused on tropical, nocturnal snakes. Temperature sensitive radiotransmitters were used to record coelomic temperatures of 11 brown tree snakes (BTS) on Guam and 5 captive animals held in a thermal mosaic. Copper models of snakes were used to characterize the climate space of BTS. Preliminary analysis suggested that captive BTS at rest chose cooler temperatures (21 - 23 °C) than those experienced by inactive wild snakes (27 - 32 °C). Free living snakes did not raise Tb by basking. Diurnal temperature profiles of resting wild snakes were similar to those of copper models placed in refugia. This suggests that, in contrast to temperate snakes, resting BTS do not actively thermoregulate. The situation for active snakes is unclear. Captive snakes with access to temperatures between 22 - 43 °C attained greater Tb while active at night (30 - 33 °C) than free ranging snakes (25 - 26 °C) limited to ambient temperatures between 24 - 26 °C. The difference in Tb might represent selection of a 30 - 33 °C Tb by captive snakes or be an artifact of movement patterns through the thermal mosaic.

22213: In the highly seasonal environments of the north temperate zone, ectothermic animals such as snakes suffer significant temporal constraints on their annual cycles, with consequences for their life histories and demographies. For example, cold winters prohibit any activity at all, but summers also may be cool, further restricting activity. In presumed evolutionary response to this, most temperate-zone snakes are viviparous; gravid females exhibit precise behavioural thermoregulation, apparently providing optimal developmental conditions for their young. However, thermoregulation often conflicts with other activities such as feeding. In fact, in many species, gravid females feed little or not at all, even in captivity. The main demographic consequences of this are reduced future reproductive output, especially through decreased reproductive frequency of individual females. Nonetheless, this tradeoff may be relatively unimportant in the long run because many snakes are long-lived "bet-hedging" species and compensate for low reproductive output in one year by surviving to reproduce at a later date. I illustrate these ideas with data for garter snakes (Thamnophis) and rattlesnakes (Crotalus).

22214: A snake community was studied in mixed prairie-woodland habitat in NE Kansas, near the junction of Douglas, Jefferson, and Leavenworth Counties, 1948-1997. 22215: Among the most critically endangered sturgeon species worldwide are those in the genus Pseudoscaphirhynchus (Scaphirhynchinae), which are endemic to the Syr Darya (P. fedtschenkoi) and Amu Darya (P. kaufmanni and P. hermanni) rivers of the Aral Sea in central Asia. All three species exhibit considerable intra-specific morphological variation. Significant differences (P < 0.05) among the three species (n = 187) were found in 15 of 17 meristic and 48 of 50 mensural characters. Principal component analysis (PCA) of meristic data and sheared PCA of mensural data provided complete or almost complete separation of these species. Eleven meristic and at least 19 mensural characters were significantly different between the narrow- and wide-snout forms of P. kaufmanni. The short- and long-snout forms of P. hermanni and P. fedtschenkoi differed significantly for 1 and 4 meristic and 37 and at least 23 mensural characters, respectively. Differences included number of fin rays, dermal plates, snout spines, and gill rakers, as well as snout, plate, fin, caudal peduncle, and barbel measurements. Sheared PCA gave complete separation between the two forms of P. fedtschenkoi, with snout, caudal peduncle, and fin measurements loading heavily. Results indicate that there are potentially six rather than three species in the genus Pseudoscaphirhynchus.

22216: Studies on north temperate fish species indicate that new habitat availability following the last glacial retreat has promoted ecological speciation in post-glacial lakes. The extensive ecophenotypic polymorphism observed among Great Lakes ciscoes suggests that they have radiated through trophic adaptation and reproductive isolation. This study aims at relating the ecomorphological and genetic polymorphisms expressed by the Lake Nipigon ciscoes assemblage in order to evaluate the likelihood of an intralacustrine divergence driven by the exploitation of alternative resources. Morphological variation, trophic and spatial niche are characterized and contrasted among four putative species (N>200). Genetic variation at 10 microsatellite loci is analysed to appraise the extent of genetic structuring and reproductive isolation among species. Our results reveal various levels of niche overlap and indicate that Coregonus artedi is more generalist than C. nigripinnis, C. hoyi and C. zenethicus. Surprisingly, trophic and morphological specialization were not as congruent as expected. Significant but low proportion of genetic variance can be attributed to differences among species allelic arrays. Globally, the results suggest that C. zenethicus and C. artedi are probably the initial colonisators of Lake Nipigon and that C. nigripinnis and C. hoyi are diverging from C. artedi through intralacustrine trophic specialization and spatial segregation.

22217: The Chinese sucker, Myxocyprinus asiaticus, is the only allotetraploid catostomid fish that is endemic to Asia. 22218: Ricefishes, known best by the medaka, Oryzias latipes, are classified in the family Adrianichthyidae in the atherinomorph order Beloniformes. The approximately twenty-five ricefish species range throughout fresh and brackish waters of eastern Eurasia, Southeast Asia, the Indian subcontinent, across the Indo-Australian archipelago, crossing Wallace's Line, to Timor. Throughout most of their range, ricefishes are small, reaching about 40 mm SL; in the tectonic lakes of Sulawesi, however, ricefishes are relative giants, reaching about 200 mm SL. Ricefishes are monophyletic and comprise two monophyletic subgroups or lineages, one large bodied and one small, diagnosed here by morphological characters. Outgroup comparison using traditional morphology supports a transformation from large to small, whereas preliminary molecular data supports a transformation from small to large. Sulawesi ricefishes are not monophyletic but, instead, include members of each of the two lineages. As expected, the sister taxa have an area of overlap, or sympatry, in Sulawesi. This distribution pattern is found in other fish taxa, supporting the idea that neither lineage is primitive to the other, but that there was a widespread ancestral taxon, and, once sister lineages diverged, some members of one or both lineages dispersed into the range of the other.

22219: Systematic relationships among three sympatric serranid sea basses from the warm temperate eastern Pacific coast, Paralabrax clathratus, P. nebulifer, and P. maculatofasciatus, are analyzed from mitochondrial DNA control region sequences and 40 allozyme loci. 22221: A search for characters was aimed at inferring phylogenetic relationships of Poeciliinae on the basis of ontogenetic changes in several structures during male maturation. 22222: A comparative histological survey of gonad structure in higher bony fishes revealed that the lobular germinal compartments in testes of all Atherinomorpha surveyed are the restricted testis type; spermatogonia are located only at the distal termini of lobules. Spermatogonia in the lobular testes of other higher teleosts are distributed along the length of the lobules (unrestricted testis type) as in, for example, the percomorph Centropomus undecimalis, snook, and the mugilomorph Mugil cephalus, black mullet. Mugil cephalus is a cosmopolitan species of importance as a food fish and for aquaculture. Stock declines of this species have occurred in Florida, but a recent net ban curtailing the commercial catch is expected to result in a rebound in the black mullet population. 22223: Divergent forms of Coregonus, with uncertain taxonomic status, co-exist in sympatry within Central Alpine lakes. 22225: A few species of frogs representing four families (Bufonidae, Dendrobatidae, Hylidae, and Leptodactylidae) inhabit elevations above 3000 m in the tropical Andes, an environment that is characterized by dramatic thermal fluctuations. 22226: Amphibians are exposed to lead (Pb) around mining sites, areas with extensive automobile traffic, and skeet ranges. Pb-exposed larvae made more trips to the surface (air-gulping) compared to unexposed larvae even under high oxygen conditions. Larvae exposed to both Pb and low oxygen displayed increased buccal ventilation compared to larvae exposed to either treatment separately. 22227: Understanding the thermal biology of ectotherms is fundamental for understanding factors that affect their movements and habitat use. 22242: Herpetologists often release animals after laboratory study in a laudable attempt at conservation. However, the subsequent fates of such animals are generally unknown. 22248: Recent geological, paleontological, morphological, and molecular studies provide identification and better definitions of the diverse clades that comprise the present American snake fauna. No single field provides a clear zoogeographic narrative of these faunal elements but the consilience of information from multiple sources offers such a base. Not unexpectedly, the oldest surviving clades are also the most ancient ones in the Americas. The typhlopids and leptotyphlopids of the Neotropics and Africa probably date from the mid-Cretaceous splitting of Gondwana by the Atlantic Ocean. The anomalepedids and Anilius in contrast are ancient South American endemics without known relatives, although the latter may be a Recent relative of the Cretaceous +Dinilysia. The Neotropical (true) boids appear to represent an ancient henophidian fauna that ranged from Madagascar across Antarctica to South America. Conversely, the American erycids, tropidophiids (and ?ungaliophiids and ?Loxocemus) derive from the Cretaceous-to-Eocene connection of eastern North America with Europe. This also may be true of the caenophidian "North American Relicts." The main American caenophidian fauna (crotalids, elapids, xenodontids, dipsadids, colubrids s.s., and natricids) did not arrive until later. 22262: Wood frogs display natural freeze tolerance during winter hibernation. 22265: The ichthyofauna in the medium and upper Rio Tocantins (Brazil) has been poorly investigated. 22266: The Trindade Island is located at 20°30'S and 29°20'W, approximately 620 nautical miles (1260 km) off the coast of Espirito Santo, forming with Martin Vaz Archipelago the most isolated insular group off the Brazilian coast. 22268: Seasonal movements of the porbeagle shark, Lamna nasus, in Canadian Atlantic waters were determined using size and sex composition of catches sampled by Fisheries Observers in the porbeagle longline fishery. 22269: Micro-PIXE (proton induced X-ray emission) analysis was used to determine the content of strontium in the core area of otoliths from Dolly Varden and Arctic char from the north slope of the Yukon Territory. 22271: Seasonality in resource availability and physiological maintenance costs may change the relationships of tradeoffs that balance to maximize fitness. 22272: Gambusia affinis and G. holbrooki from localities like Illinois, North Carolina, and New Jersey stop reproducing in late July to mid-August, when there may be up to two months of mild weather remaining in the season. We tested this hypothesis with enclosure experiments in which we evaluated three components of fitness of newborn young as a function of their date of birth. At four times during the summer, we set out 20 offspring from ten different litters in ten different enclosures, then estimated the probability of survival to maturity, age at maturity and fecundity in the first litter. The last outplant date was after the usual end of the reproductive season and represents the hypothetical last litter of the season. We obtained these litters by keeping females in the laboratory with long photoperiods and high water temperatures. Our results, duplicated in two seasons, demonstrate that the earliest born young have a much higher probability of survival to maturity and much more rapid development than those born late in the season. 22273: We determined the variability in year class and brood-specific growth and mortality rates of first-year smallmouth bass (Micropterus dolomieu) and assessed the importance of temperature and spawning date to growth and survival. 22274: The timing and duration of spawning in smallmouth bass populations are closely tied to body size and spring warming rates. 22275: Correlations between breeding date and the life history or energy stores of individuals might arise owing to two different mechanisms: condition dependence or adaptation-by-time. It seems poorly-suited, however, to some semelparous, capital breeding species that have less flexible breeding times. 22276: Seasonality leads to time constraints on the major life history transitions. 22277: The seasonal timing of reproduction may vary with individual characteristics (or 'state variables'), such as size and energetic state. I review this phenomenon in fishes. 22280: Classic descriptive and functional studies of ophidian feeding have resulted in a detailed, and supported, hypothesis for the mechanics of prey ingestion in snakes.
