22285: Gordon Walls (1940, 1942) constructed an elegant, logical story for the early origin of snakes as burrowers, based upon the anatomy of the eye. Independently, Mahendra (1938) suggested that burrowing snakes, such as Typhlops, represented the most basal snake lineages, also underscoring the hypothesis of a fossorial ancestry for snakes. This hypothesis, with some modification, has been widely accepted (Underwood, 1970; Rieppel, 1988). Recent phylogenetic research by Caldwell and Lee (1997) suggested an alternative to the fossorial ancestor hypothesis, reviving an early hypothesis for an aquatic origin of modern snakes. Can the ophthalmic characteristics so forcefully argued by Walls for a fossorial origin of snakes equally support an argument for an aquatic origin for snakes? In fact, many of these same ophthalmic characteristics are observed in aquatic taxa. The shape and relative size of the lens and the method of accommodation in modern snakes are typical of aquatic animals and suggest an aquatic ancestry for snakes. Other characteristics of the eye are less obviously attributable to an aquatic ancestor but are still consistent with this alternative hypothesis. In light of the revised historical framework, this alternative hypothesis for the ecological origin for snakes merits closer inspection.

22286: Diamondback terrapins, Malaclemys terrapin, frequently drown due to incidental capture in crab pots. 22287: The gopher tortoise (Gopherus polyphemus) is legally protected by state regulations throughout its range and federally listed as threatened in the western portion of its range. 22288: Geochelone sulcata (Cryptodira: Testudinidae) achieves a length of 830 mm and weight of 105.5 kg, and is the largest of the world's continental tortoises. 22289: We investigated populations of the Jamaican slider turtle (Trachemys terrapen), a species endemic to Jamaica. 22290: Few studies have addressed intraspecific trends within a marine turtle species over a large area. 22291: The five-lined skink is widely distributed in eastern North America but its populations are disjunct and of conservation concern in the northern portion of its range. 22292: Road mortality is becoming an increasing threat to endangered and isolated reptile populations. 22294: The copperbelly is federally listed under the Endangered Species Act as Threatened in the northern part of its range, and protected to the south by the Copperbelly Water Snake Conservation Agreement. 22295: The copperbelly is an inhabitant of shallow wetlands in parts of the midwestern United States. 22296: From 1979-1983 we conducted radiotelemetry and mark-recapture studies on massasauga rattlesnakes (Sistrurus catenatus) at the Squaw Creek National Wildlife Refuge in northwestern Missouri. 22297: Much of central Florida has been subjected to strip mining for phosphate. The mining process drastically alters the upland habitats available for wildlife occupancy. Thirteen species of amphibians (4) and reptiles (9) were determined to be "focal species," that is, they were under-represented at the reclaimed mine sites, relative to the unmined sites. Reasons for their under-representation include the lack of suitable substrate for burrowing species, lack of temporary ponds for amphibian reproduction, and lack of sufficient litter, ground cover, and plant structure for other species. Plans to further study selected focal species, including translocating common species to reclaimed habitats will be reviewed.

22298: Hubbs and Miller's research on the Great Basin emphasized changes at the level of races and subspecies; these changes apparently occurred rapidly, in hundreds to thousands of years. Miocene to Pleistocene fossils of these fishes, in contrast, suggest unexpectedly slow changes at the species level, i.e., over hundreds of thousands to nearly 10 million years, with infrequent evolution of new species. Resolution of this incongruence requires clarification of the relative frequency of short-term differentiation, species origins, and extinction. The Great Basin evidence demonstrates that fluctuating pluvial-interpluvial cycles result in rapid proliferation of new subspecies but eventual extinction of all but generalist survivors, often as relict endemics. The frequent extinctions and infrequent persistence of new species in the Great Basin seem to be the consequence of repeated loss of habitat during interpluvial stages of Pleistocene cycles. The result seems to be rapid but superficial changes in morphology without long-term change. Great Basin fish faunas exhibit low diversity and high endemism characteristic of tectonically active areas. The low diversity suggests that high extinction rates were caused by high elevations, high gradients (low habitat diversity), and climatic variability.

22299: Anchovies (genus Engraulis) inhabit temperate upwelling zones and boundary currents across the globe, including locations in Europe (E. encrasicolus), southern Africa (E. capensis), Australia (E. australis), Japan (E. japonicus), Mexico-California (E. mordax), Chile-Peru (E. ringens), and Argentina-Brazil (E. anchoita). Comparisons of mtDNA cytochrome b sequences reveal four major lineages corresponding to three New World species and a single lineage including all four Old World species. The relationships among haplotypes in the Old World anchovies demonstrate recent colonization events between Japan and Australia, and between Europe and southern Africa. A previous population in southern Africa (possibly the progenitor of the European population) may have gone extinct and been recently recolonized from Europe. A comparison of anchovies to sardines (genus Sardinops), which have a similar geographic distribution, reveals a dramatically different distribution of mtDNA lineages. These data prompt two conclusions about the biogeography of temperate marine fishes. First, a vicariance model alone is inadequate to explain the distribution of evolutionary lineages in these taxa. Both vicariance and dispersal events are strongly implicated. Second, the principle of generalized tracks, in which species with similar distributions have similar evolutionary histories, is contradicted by a comparison of phylogeographic patterns in sardines and anchovies.

22300: The plains killifish, Fundulus zebrinus, is a smallish cyprinodontid fish found throughout the western plains states, and additionally it has been introduced to the Colorado River drainage. 22302: Flatfishes of the family Pleuronectidae are distributed in marine waters across the entire northern hemisphere. The majority of species (49 out of 59) are found in the Pacific Ocean with only ten pleuronectid species in the Atlantic Ocean. 22303: The variable platyfish, Xiphophorus variatus, has the broadest range of any species of Xiphophorus. Most work on this species has concentrated on populations in the Rio Tamesi drainage, towards the northern end of its distribution. Here, we report on the populations toward the southern end of the range, in the Rios Nautla, Solteros, Tecolutla and Cazones. One variety, termed Sangre de Cristo in the aquarium literature, is characterized by deep red coloration on the belly and throat of adult males. Another color variety is vivid yellow coloration of the gonopodium. These color variants, and others, are extremely restricted in geographic distribution. Sangre de Cristo occurs in an area no larger than ten by fifteen kilometers, with the frequency of the variant highest towards the center of the range. 22305: Lake Pontchartrain, a complex, warm-temperate, shallow basin, is one of the largest estuaries in the Gulf of Mexico region. Water temperature, salinity, pH, current direction, wind velocity and lunar cycles were recorded for all tows. Data were analyzed using 3-way ANOVA. Preliminary results show increased densities inshore, with predictable cycling over the sampling period. Fluctuations in physical parameters appear to affect inshore and offshore larval distributions and abundances. This information will aid in predicting settlement for future recruitment into local populations.

22311: A system that analyzes and displays spatially referenced data is known as a geographical information system (GIS). The use of GIS technology has facilitated understanding of complex relationships between organisms and their environment. In ichthyology, GIS could facilitate access to information associated with taxonomic collections. It could provide spatial analysis within and among species using distribution patterns of morphological and genetic characters; accurately analyze geographical distributions of morphological characters and correlate them with ecological parameters; and provide an objective measurement of the status of an ecosystem, which has generally been done based on human perception but lacked data. Taxonomic collections of voucher and type specimens and their associated environmental data are abundant sources of unexplored information. This information is highly relevant for management of natural resources because taxonomy has been built upon it. This information, when analyzed with GIS, could be used to address these areas and to provide the foundation for measuring fish biodiversity and evaluating the dynamics of spatio-temporal patterns of fish. The FDEP's FMRI is applying GIS technology to analyse the robust databases associated with its voucher collections. Further study of voucher specimens will allow us to produce maps of morphological characteristics of fish linked to ecological parameters. We also intend to produce synthesized information for ecosystem management in a format amenable to spatial- and time-analysis study.

22312: If Pacific salmon are a cultural icon, then their treatment in the past century is certainly inconsistent with this value. Recent reviews of their status in Canada and the Pacific northwest report about 1,000 populations extinct or at risk, and several stocks are listed or proposed for listing under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. Causes of the declines are numerous, usually attributed to someone or something else, and always debatable. The history of impacts can be broadly characterized as: an initial uninformed and rapid expansion of fisheries; then decades of rapid economic expansion in many sectors plus heightened competitive over-fishing of hatchery and wild salmonids; and finally, 20-30 years of extensive regulation, confrontation, and change. During the latter period, the issue of "borders" in management and conservation has become very evident. The Pacific Salmon Treaty between the United States and Canada (1985) provided the first comprehensive agreement on Pacific salmon and offered a means to cooperate in conservation and development. Unfortunately, it now exemplifies the problem of borders and their risk to biodiversity in Pacific salmon. This talk will address the history of salmon conflicts, the complexity of salmon issues, and describe the risks associated with the present Treaty impasse.

22313: Atlantic swordfish are a highly migratory species targeted by domestic and international fishing fleets in the North and South Atlantic Oceans. The 22-member International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) conducts stock assessments and issues management recommendations for swordfish fisheries. In 1996, the North Atlantic swordfish stock was estimated to be at 58% of the biomass needed to produce maximum sustainable yield. In 1997, the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) identified North Atlantic swordfish as overfished and began developing a domestic swordfish rebuilding program under the authority of the Magnuson Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act. This plan may include time/area closures (to limit catch of undersized fish) and import restrictions. In 1997, U.S. swordfish imports totaled more than 15,000 mt and were worth more than US$95 million. As a major importer of swordfish, the U.S. can play a role in international conservation by ensuring that imports are from countries participating in the ICCAT conservation program. NMFS will continue to pursue domestic strategies to rebuild this stock and will work within ICCAT to support international rebuilding strategies. It is not clear what effect restrictions on U.S. fishermen may have in light of increasing international fishing efforts on this highly migratory species.

22314: Initially, under the auspices of the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) Interstate Fisheries Management Program, and subsequently the operation of the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission (ASMFC), striped bass (Morone saxatilis) management of the mid-Atlantic (Virginia-Maine) stocks have showed both an initial abysmal beginning, and a final and unique result that can claim responsibility for the dramatic recovery of the heavily fished mid-Atlantic stocks. Recommendations were made to the ASMFC as early as 1942 for the need for more stringent unified regulations that transcended state boundaries; but it was not until 1981 that a Scientific and Statistics Committee recommended to the ASMFC Striped Bass Board that the spawning grounds be closed during the spawning season, and that the minimum size limit be 14" coast-wide; while most of the states adopted such measures in 1982 their enforcement was voluntary. It was not until the passage of the Federal Atlantic Striped Bass Conservation Act in 1984, requiring full compliance with the Act, that each state fulfilled their obligations. Subsequently, a combination of protective regulations and stringent enforcement, coincident with several highly successful dominant year classes (1987, 1989, 1993, and 1996) have led to an unprecedented abundance of large (>24", 600 mm) fish. So successful is the program that Congress has passed subsequent coast-wide legislation (Atlantic Coast Cooperative Fisheries Conservation and Management Act of 1994) to protect other coastal migratory species.

22315: Mitochondrial DNA has proven useful for the elucidation of population structure and questions regarding the behavior of adult female marine turtles. What can the analysis of multiple distinct foraging sites tell us about marine turtle developmental habitats and movements in the Caribbean? Analyses of juvenile foraging populations have provided information regarding recruitment scales in the Caribbean and Atlantic. Previous studies indicate that multiple nesting locations contribute individuals to a particular foraging site. Oftentimes these foraging sites are located outside the geopolitical boundaries of countries supporting the nesting populations. Determination of the composition of juvenile and adult foraging grounds provide information on movement and behavior of marine turtles in the Caribbean and Atlantic. Consequently, this information is necessary for the development of management policies directed towards marine turtles. Migratory behavior of marine organisms forces scientists and management organizations to think differently about how conservation efforts should be directed. Finally, unawareness of human delineated boundaries emphasizes the importance of international cooperation in the maintenance of biodiversity.

22316: Kemp's ridley sea turtles (Lepidochelys kempi) nested in the tens of thousands in the 1940's and were the most abundant species in the Gulf of Mexico. Intensive egg harvest and mortality at sea caused the population to plummet; by the mid-1970's, less than 1000 nests per year were counted at Rancho Nuevo, Mexico, the only known nesting beach. Efforts to prevent extinction were initiated in Mexico in 1960s, and from 1966-1978 approximately 30,000 hatchlings were released per year. A United States-Mexico cooperative research and conservation program was formed in 1978 which now protects 95% of the nests laid at Rancho Nuevo. The cooperative includes the Mexican Ministry of Fisheries, U.S. National Parks Service, Fish and Wildlife Service, and National Marine Fisheries Service. Additional research support and funding comes from the Gladys Porter Zoo in Brownsville, the Texas Shrimpers Association and other groups. The National Marine Fisheries Service sponsored a captive rearing program and efforts to re-establish a nesting colony at South Padre Island, Texas. Both nations passed legislation that requires Turtle Excluder Devices on shrimp trawling gear to reduce incidental mortality. Today the Kemp's ridley population is still more than an order of magnitude below historical levels, but nests are increasing, largely due to the dedicated efforts of two nations.

22317: Hydrogeology of the highly karstic and arid Texas-Mexico border region is complex, and subterranean hydrographic relationships poorly understood, yet these aquifers are heavily exploited for municipal, industrial and agricultural uses. Diverse contaminants problems in the Rio Grande (= Rio Bravo) are well known, and increasing development, especially in the border corridor, and regional large-scale pumping of aquifers, are rapidly increasing threats to environmental health in the region. Preliminary hydrogeologic data indicating that karst flows may pass under the Rio Grande were presented during international impact assessment hearings for a proposed hazardous waste dump in south Texas. We apply phylogenetic and biogeographic relationships of the regional troglobitic fauna, together with genetic distance data, as potentially convenient, quick, and relatively inexpensive, indirect measures of degree of hydrologic interconnections among aquifers, and thus as indicators of probabilities and geographic extent of impacts from leakage from the waste dump in Texas, or any other aquifer impact, such as excessive withdrawals. Sequence data from mtDNA of populations of Prietella phreatophila throughout a large region of Coahuila indicate considerable historic and/or current connections among populations, as do distributions of less-thoroughly studied troglobitic invertebrates broadly sympatric with this obligate cave catfish. Invertebrate distributions also support the hypothesis of trans-border subterranean aquifer connections under the Rio Grande. Future studies will seek increased resolution of relationships among Prietella populations, and phylogenetic hypotheses of relationships of the troglobitic invertebrates, to further corroborate these preliminary conclusions.

22318: Fishes of the Rio Conchos and Rio Grande and their tributaries were surveyed from 1992 to 1995 and these collections were compared to historical surveys. Cluster analysis of fish assemblages revealed several distinguishable but overlapping assemblage structures. Two spring localities, both impacted, were dominated by Gambusia, as were headwater localities of Rio Conchos tributaries. Lower Rio Conchos tributary localities were more diverse and had large numbers of Notropis jemezanus, Campostoma ornatum, and Gambusia senilis. Mainstem assemblages near the Rio Conchos/Rio Grande confluence were characterized by a diverse cyprinid component in addition to ictalurids and the Mexican tetra, and few introduced species. Other mainstem sites that were heavily impacted by channelization and agricultural runoff were dominated by Cyprinella lutrensis and had large numbers of introduced Tilapia. Lower canyons of the Rio Grande were characterized by a diverse fauna that included both swift water species such as Rhinichthys cataractae and Macrhybopsis aestivalis as well as other species characteristic of the Chihuahuan Desert rivers. Comparison of recent to historical collections revealed substantial changes in assemblage composition in many reaches, often due to population reduction or extirpation of species.

22319: Most often measures of biodiversity have been documented and expressed in regard to political boundaries, as opposed to ecological areas. There have been extensive programs of intentional introductions of nonindigenous species by agencies in one political area without prior consultation with adjacent political areas. When this situation involves international boundaries it can lead to greater concern. The present freshwater fish fauna of Canada could be said to result totally from fishes that have "invaded or reinvaded" Canadian waters as those waters appeared. The process continues today. Records starting in 1949 indicate that at least eight species have entered Canadian waters by moving across or around the Great Lakes and interconnecting rivers. The list includes eight species native to the United States and seven introduced there. If we include the potential of global warming there are an additional 41 species to the immediate south of Canada that might invade. If we extend the list to the whole of Canada and the United States there is a total of 63 species that have achieved part of their distribution by this vector.

22320: The northern range limit of a species is the dynamic result of local extinction versus establishment of new populations. This, in turn, is dependent upon dispersal, habitat availability, habitat predictability, population dynamics, and metapopulation dynamics. In Canada, all native species of amphibians reach their northern limits. For some, this limit lies just inside the southern Canadian border and therefore these species are candidates for Canada's endangered species list whatever their distribution or abundance in the United States. Canada has no endemic amphibian species. To what extent are these Canadian endangered species an artifact of the position of the Canada/US border? Or, in consideration of the genetic distinction and isolation that may occur among northern limital populations, how much of a biological imperative does designation of "endangered" in Canada carry? These questions are best addressed on a case by case basis.

22322: Forty years ago, Bleakney pointed out that the factors limiting the ranges of herpetofauna had not been well studied. This is still true. Presumably, limits are set by extreme climatic conditions in some if not all cases. The northern limits are set by the severity of cold temperatures in winter or by the impact of summer temperatures on the development of the embryos. The northern limits of most Canadian reptiles are remarkably similar, especially compared to the variation observed in amphibians. Few reptiles tolerate freezing, and in those that do the ecological importance of this ability is not obvious. There is some evidence of latitudinal trends in physiological traits and patterns of growth that suggest adaptation to cooler, shorter summers in northern reptiles, but not much evidence of adaptation of pivotal temperatures of environmental sex determination, or to low incubation temperatures, nor to colder winters. I will discuss evidence suggesting that the northern distribution of reptiles is determined largely by the length and warmth of the summer.

22323: At least five species of frogs from North America survive extensive freezing of their body fluids. Their limits of tolerance emanate from the combined interactions of freeze temperature and the duration of exposure. Frogs protect their tissues from injury by accumulating massive quantities of glucose or glycerol and by relocating body water from major organs. The roles of physiological systems in the cryobiology of these frogs are varied. Some morphological characteristics and systemic functions are key elements supporting freeze tolerance. For example, the integument transmits ice crystals into body fluids preventing extensive supercooling of body fluids and the cardiovascular system actively distributes cryoprotectant from central stores in the liver to other body tissues before arresting. In contrast, the CNS and skeletal muscle function at temporarily reduced rates upon thawing that are in proportion to the intensity of the freeze episode. This then may affect important organismal activities such as the ability of frogs to find and interact with mates.

22324: Various species of terrestrially-hibernating amphibians and reptiles are freeze tolerant, enduring long-term freezing exposures with as much as 50-65% of total body water frozen as extracellular ice. Studies in my lab explore the biochemical adaptations underlying natural freeze tolerance. Recent studies have included analysis of the hormone, B-adrenergic receptor, and second messenger responses underlying cryoprotectant (glucose) production by liver and identified a novel form of insulin in wood frogs. Other studies have made the first analysis of freeze-induced gene expression in vertebrate organs. Using a cDNA library constructed from liver of wood frogs (Rana sylvatica) frozen for 24 h at -2.5 degrees C, we identified the freeze-induced upregulation of genes coding for the a and S subunits of fibrinogen (a plasma clotting protein), the mitochondrial membrane ADP/ATP translocase, and a novel protein (about 90 amino acids, 10 kD) with a nuclear exporting sequence. Northern hybridization analysis showed that mRNA levels for all three proteins (fibrinogen subunits paralleled each other) had distinct organ-specific patterns and responded differently to freeze/thaw, dehydration, and anoxia stresses. Other studies have revealed that genes that are anoxia-induced in freshwater turtles are also upregulated by freezing in hatchling painted turtles.

22325: Hatchling freeze tolerance has been reported in western painted turtles (NE and various Canadian), midland painted turtles (Ontario and OH), eastern X midland painted turtles (NJ), and ornate box turtles (NE). Lack of hatchling freeze tolerance has been reported in red eared sliders (IL and LA), spiny soft-shelled turtles (NE), yellow mud turtles (NE), and snapping turtles (NE). To this list I add wood turtles and common map turtles (IN) as not freeze tolerant, and very preliminary data suggests that southern painted turtles (LA) are also freeze intolerant, while Blanding's turtles appear to be freeze tolerant. Understanding the evolution of this trait is complicated for several reasons. These include 1. disagreement over the importance of freeze tolerance vs supercooling in natural situations, 2. lack of a consistent standard for defining freeze tolerance, 3. lack of comparable interpopulational freeze tolerance data for a species with large latitudinal range and possible variation in this trait, and, 4. lack of a phylogenetic analysis of a clade with variation in this trait. More work is needed.

22326: It has long been a mystery how aquatically overwintering frogs, such as bullfrogs, survive winter hypoxia. There have been anecdotal reports that frogs bury in mud, but anoxic frogs survived less than two weeks at 4°C in the laboratory, and frogs did not bury in mud when it was available. In the field, while most of the pond bottom was severely hypoxic, the frogs were found in very cold (0-1°) and relatively well oxygenated water at the extreme edge of the pond, centimetres below ice cover. In the laboratory, frogs in a thermal gradient chose colder temperatures when the water was hypoxic (Tattersall and Boutilier; J. Exp. Biol. 200:1031-1038). Frogs have a high Q10 (around 5) below 4°C, thus metabolism is reduced in cold water at the pond edge. Finally, the metabolic rate of overwintering frogs in hypoxic water gradually decreased by 60% over several weeks, reducing fuel consumption and the amount of oxygen required in the water (Donohoe and Boutilier, J. Exp. Biol, in press). Aquatic frogs thus remain aerobic all winter by choosing a low environmental temperature to reduce metabolic rate, choosing water with the highest available oxygen, and reducing metabolic rate at a constant temperature.
22327: Several terrestrial anurans and reptiles that live at high latitudes have developed elaborate physiological and biochemical mechanisms for surviving cold winter temperatures. These animals can endure the conversion of up to 65% of their total body water into extracellular ice and then revive after freezing solid for days or weeks. Several studies have indicated an important role for reversible protein phosphorylation in the regulation of freeze-induced metabolic adaptations and documented changing patterns of activity of protein kinases A and C. New studies are examining the roles of mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinases in signal transduction in freeze-tolerant and anoxia-tolerant frogs and turtles. Stress- and organ-specific changes have been found in the responses of the extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERKs), the stress-activated protein kinases (SAPKs), and p38 that indicate differential functions in cell response to stress. Other studies have monitored stress-induced changes in transcription factors by Western blotting and electrophoretic mobility shift assays; these bind to DNA at the promoter regions of their target genes and induce gene expression in response to cellular stress. The patterns of MAP kinase activation in stress-tolerant animals suggest the importance of these modules in adapting to oxygen deprivation and severe osmotic stress and identify freezing as a novel activator of MAP kinases.

22328: The 98,000-hectare Lake Songkhla wetland complex is one of Thailand's most unique and important natural resources. It is home to one of the most taxonomically diverse assemblages of aquatic snakes in the world. One species of true sea snake (Hydrophis brookii), one species of file snake (Acrochordus granulatus), and several species of Asian water snakes (Homalopsinae) live here. We trapped, marked, and released 236 rainbow water snakes (Enhydris enhydris) on 13 consecutive days in a marsh near the village of Ban Tha Hin. A total of 380 snakes were trapped in a 1.5 ha area and of these 144 were previously marked. Schumacher's estimate of the population size is 473 snakes (95% confidence limits = 406 to 567 snakes) and the Schnabel binomial estimate using the poisson approximation is 446 snakes (95% confidence limits = 371 to 561 snakes). Enhydris enhydris spends the majority of its time in the mud-root-tangle at the edge of ditches, pools and canals. Our observations indicate that most snakes are found in a one meter wide band along the aquatic edges. We estimate the linear density of Enhydris enhydris to be approximately 0.5 snakes per square meter of shoreline.

22329: We conducted a radiotelemetric study of aquatic snakes in a wetland meadow in Lake Songkhla, Thailand. 22330: Studies of the affects of natural variation in food availability may provide valuable insight regarding mechanisms that govern population dynamics and the responses of individuals to environmental change. The use of telemetry in large bodied snakes such as the timber rattlesnake allows simultaneous monitoring of multiple responses to changes in the environment. I monitored feeding rates, growth, reproductive activities, time allocation, and field metabolic rates in a sample of radiotagged timber rattlesnakes during a high and low resource year. In 1996, thirteen radiotagged timber rattlesnakes exhibited lower feeding rates than ten radiotagged snakes during 1997. Snakes exhibited significantly greater size-adjusted growth rates during 1997. During the low resource year, no reproductive activities were observed, however, under conditions of high feeding rates, fourteen independent reproductive associations were observed among 10 radiotagged snakes. Snakes in low resource conditions spent a higher proportion of available daylight time engaged in foraging, whereas, under high resource conditions, snakes spent more time in resting and reproductive activities. An understanding of these dependencies will allow greater accuracy in the prediction of responses of individuals and populations to changes in the environment.

22331: We explored the issue of predator specialization by examining dietary variation in the widespread North American long-nosed snake, Rhinocheilus lecontei. We examined the stomach contents of more than 800 museum specimens, and supplemented our findings with published dietary records. Sixty-six percent of 134 prey eaten by R. lecontei were lizards, 26% were mammals, and 6% were squamate eggs; teiid lizards of the genus Cnemidophorus comprised 72% of all lizard prey. 22332: Predation by introduced vertebrates caused the near extinction of the giant lizard of the Canarian island of El Hierro, Gallotia simonyi (Sauria, Lacertidae). Thus, antipredator behavior such as escape (sprint performance) may have played a major role. We studied temperature dependent sprint performance in the captive population of the giant lizard and we compared performance with G. caesaris, a small-sized lizard abundant throughout El Hierro, and with G. stehlini, an abundant large sized lizard from the island of Gran Canaria. Among adults, maximum speed was significantly higher in the G. stehlini, both in absolute (m/s) and relative speed (SVL/s). G. simonyi and the smaller sympatric G. caesaris did not differ significantly in maximum speeds (m/s). Juvenile G. simonyi were slower than juvenile G. stehlini but the differences were significant only in absolute speed (m/s). Juvenile G. simonyi were significantly slower than similar sized adult G. caesaris. Adults from the captive population of G. simonyi should not be used for reintroduction because their sprint performance may have been hampered by prolonged captivity. Juveniles could be released although introduced predators should be closely monitored due to the lower sprint performance of juvenile G. simonyi compared to the similar sized adult G. caesaris which are abundant in the reintroduction area.

22333: In 1983 Anderson and colleagues proposed that radial arrays of traps (trapping webs) could be used to estimate absolute population density of trappable species, in a manner analogous to the visual/auditory circular plots widely used for estimating densities of passerine birds. We tested the validity of this approach by setting radial arrays of glueboards for lizards in forested areas of Guam and Saipan islands prior to or shortly after conducting total removal sampling for the same species in the same areas. One of two skink species sampled, Carlia fusca, is readily trapped and may be attracted to traps by previously-caught conspecifics. The abundance estimate for this species, as estimated by five trapping webs, exceeded the estimate provided by total removal in three cases and was less than the total removal estimate in two others. The density of the other lizard species sampled, Emoia caeruleocauda, was grossly underestimated by three trapping webs. On days of suitable weather (e.g., sunshine for heliophils) trapping webs may provide useful, if imprecise, estimates of absolute abundance for species that are abundant, readily trapped, terrestrial, and relatively uniform in distribution.

22334: The Cuban brown anole (Anolis sagrei) was introduced into south Florida about 50 years ago, and is now arguably the most numerous terrestrial vertebrate on the peninsula. This, along with habitat alteration, coincides with the decline of the native green anole (Anolis carolinensis) in Florida. To experimentally assess the brown anole's role in the decline, I introduced brown anoles onto three dredge spoil islands occupied by greens, and used three islands with native greens as controls. Islands contained forested and non-forested habitats. Populations were monitored for four years with capture-mark-recapture techniques, and detailed microhabitat and spatial data was collected. Green anole control population sizes and habitat use parameters remained stable, whereas treatment populations crashed, and the few remaining greens utilized different habitat types than their ancestors. 22335: The highly arboreal gray rat snake (Elaphe obsoleta spiloides) is a significant predator upon endangered red-cockaded woodpeckers (RCWs) (Picoides borealis). Snake excluder traps were used to determine selectivity for RCW nest trees, active roost trees, inactive roost trees and within cluster and outside cluster random trees by capturing snakes attempting to climb trees. 22336: The brown tree snake (BTS, Boiga irregularis) was accidentally introduced on Guam approximately 50 years ago, and has caused major ecological and economic impacts. As a result, much research has been devoted to the biology of this nocturnal, arboreal snake. Each snake was followed for 9-13 consecutive days. Each morning we tracked each snake to its refuge, visually sighting most of them. We characterized each refuge, and obtained data on the temperature inside many using Hobo loggers, inserted into the refugium after the snake left. We also conducted a survey of the vegetation at our study site, to compare utilization with availability. About 90% of 127 refugia were above ground, typically in trees. Snake refugium use was not random. BTSs strongly preferred some species (e.g. Pandanus provided 72.4% of refuges, but only comprised about 6.5% of canopy cover). This choice may be related to the thermal and hydric environment provided by this unusual tree. We discuss these preferences and some of their implications.

22337: In southwestern New Mexico's Chihuahuan Desert, Gila monsters (Heloderma suspectum) may avoid extreme environmental conditions in underground shelters. Because shelters that are suitable during cold winter months may not be so during the hot and dry summer, we investigated differences in shelter use across seasons. No differences were detected in entrance dimensions, but shelters used in the fall and winter were deeper than those of the spring and summer. Spring and winter shelters were frequently in rocky substrata, while summer shelters were more typically in better developed soils. Winter shelter entrances were strongly oriented toward the south, while those of other seasons were more variable in orientation. Slopes containing winter shelters also were strongly oriented toward the south, while those of spring and summer shelters were oriented toward the east and southeast. We explored relationships between the physical attributes of shelters and their microclimates (temperature and humidity) using miniature data loggers. Winter shelters provided warmer microclimates during the winter, while summer shelters provided more humidity during the summer, when compared to shelters from other seasons. A large proportion of winter shelters are reused, suggesting that suitable winter shelters are relatively less common than shelters suitable for use in other seasons.

22338: A field study of the relationship between female size and clutch depth in Podocnemis expansa was carried out at the Middle Caqueta River, Colombian Amazonia. Measurements of width and diagonal of the trails left by the females on the sand were used as surrogates of female size. Clutch and egg sizes were also studied as well as the relationship to female size. Larger females laid more and larger eggs which were buried deeper. Effects of nest depth on sex ratios are discussed together with implications for lifetime sex ratios produced by females and population sex ratios in nature. Data showed no evidence supporting the Optimal Propagule Size models in this fresh water turtle. No evidence was found of small females producing suboptimal size eggs.

22339: Desert tortoises (Gopherus agassizii) retreat to hibernacula during winter months in the northern part of their range. We studied hibernation behavior and quantified hibernaculum characteristics of radio-telemetered tortoises at two sites in the northeastern Mojave Desert. These sites differ in elevation, physiognomy and vegetation. Miniature temperature-recording data loggers were attached to these tortoises previous to the onset of hibernation and removed after emergence in 1995-1996 (n=13) and in 1996-1997 (n=16). The average hibernation onset dates were: 4 Nov 95 (SD=12.24 days) and 24 Oct 96 (SD=7.99 days). The average hibernation termination dates were 24 Mar 96 (SD=14.59 days) and 13 Mar 97 (SD=4.37 days). These dates were significantly different between the two hibernation seasons (onset: P=0.0058; termination: P=0.009). The duration of hibernation was not significantly different between sites, genders and seasons. Two tortoises experienced ambient temperatures below 0 degrees C (#464 < 2 hours; #5131 < 4 hours) while outside their hibernacula in April 1997 and survived. All air temperatures inside hibernacula remained above 2 degrees C. The hibernacula at one site were investigated with a fiberoptic light scope to determine depths that tortoises occupied. Correlations are made between hibernacula temperatures and the depth of the tortoises.

22340: Hybridization events between species and genera of emydid turtles are rarely reported. Putative hybrids reported here include crosses between Clemmys insculpta and Emydoidea blandingii, Graptemys sp. and Trachemys scripta, and Pseudemys sp. and Trachemys scripta. Intergeneric matings took place under captive conditions, although in large outdoor semi-natural enclosures. Supporting data on parentage from mitochondrial and nuclear DNA analyses will be also be presented. The Clemmys X Emydoidea hybrids display a blending of parental characteristics; expression of certain morphological and behavioral traits may, speculatively, represent traits that were present in a common ancestor of the parental species. Living hybrid specimens will be studied to determine rates of fertility and ontogeny of morphological and behavioral characters. Should these hybrids prove to be fertile, crosses will be initiated in order to follow the segregation of traits defining these different Emydid genera.

22341: Blanding's turtles and spotted turtles are listed as Endangered by the state of Indiana. We are using telemetry to study their habitat use and patterns of movement in a wetland complex in the Pigeon River Fish and Wildlife Area, in northeastern Indiana. Home range analysis revealed that individuals used extensive areas, but also exhibited fidelity to particular sites. Spotted turtles were most often observed in shallow vegetation patches dominated by sedges, cattail, and small shrubs. Blanding's turtles, however, used a relatively broader range of microhabitats, including open water, scrub-shrub and areas dominated by lilypads and sedges. They also tended to use deeper areas than spotted turtles. Movement between wetlands and terrestrial activity was observed in both species of varying degrees. In addition to summarizing our findings on habitat use and home ranges, we will discuss the implications of these findings for conserving the species.

22342: The vermilion snapper (Lutjanidae: Rhomboplites aurorubens) is an important species to commercial and recreational fishers in the southeastern United States, especially in the northern Gulf of Mexico and off the coast of the Carolinas in the South Atlantic Bight (SAB). A recent publication by Cuellar et al. was the first to use the most effective techniques on reproduction of multiple-spawning fishes (from Hunter et al. 1985, and Hunter and Macewicz 1985) on vermilion snapper, from samples taken during 1992 and 1993 from the SAB. We used similar techniques as those used by Cuellar et al. (1996) on 1,962 vermilion snapper ranging from 195 to 570 mm total length during 1991-1994 from the northeastern Gulf of Mexico (NEGOM). Most (70%) of our fish were sampled from the recreational catch and fishing-depth was 31 to 98 m. We estimated that 1993-1994 sex ratio was 1:1, batch fecundity was 26,761-415,161 hydrated oocytes, average-annual spawning frequency was 44 in 1993 and 23 in 1994, and annual fecundity was 0.62-21.9 million. Our estimates of batch fecundity, spawning frequency and annual fecundity were all greater (at fish length) than for SAB vermilion snapper (Cuellar et al. 1996). Possible causes of these differences are water temperature, preservation, diet, length of spawning season, and sampling techniques.

22343: Histological examination of gonad tissue from 1300 specimens showed that blackbelly rosefish have intraovarian gestation. Fertilization is internal, as free spermatozoa were found primarily in resting ovaries from July through December with peak occurrence in September through November. There was a delay of one to three months before fertilization, as oocyte development did not begin until December. Occurrence during January through April of early-celled embryos, the most advanced stage observed, and postovulatory follicles indicated that oocyte development was rapid. Embryos composed of a blastodermal cap and a large yolk mass were surrounded by a clear gelatinous matrix within the ovary. The reproductive mode in blackbelly rosefish appeared to be intermediate between oviparity and viviparity.

22344: Previous results have demonstrated that females within the subfamily Glandulocaudinae (family Characidae) are inseminated. With the exception of one genus that transfers sperm with spherical nuclei ('aquasperm') to the female, the species of all other genera transfer sperm with elongated nuclei. We have been carrying out transmission electron microscopy on the testes of available species in order to describe the morphology of the mature sperm and to ascertain the mechanisms of nuclear elongation. Additionally, our results have uncovered potential characters that may prove useful in hypothesizing phylogenetic relationships among these taxa. Within the Glandulocaudinae, the mature spermatozoa of the genera Diapoma, Hysteronotus, Corynopoma and Pseudocorynopoma all have the anterior portion of the flagellum contained within an elongated cytoplasmic collar. The mature spermatozoa of Mimagoniates barberi, M. microlepis and M. rheocharis, on the other hand, have very short cytoplasmic collars with the flagellum free along most of its length. However, an analysis of spermiogenesis in these three species showed that during spermatid development, the cytoplasmic collar (containing the flagellum) initially elongates substantially, but subsequently most of the collar degenerates before maturation is complete. Therefore, for the species thus far analyzed, an elongated cytoplasmic collar at least at some point during development may be a synapomorphy.

22345: Poecilia formosa is known as an all-female species which reproduces gynogenetically. Normally sperm from closely related species trigger the embryogenesis. After breeding Poecilia formosa for 10 years in our laboratory now, we found phenotypic males for the first time last year. The most important question now is whether the masculinized fish are functional Poecilia formosa males which can even reproduce or if they occur because of an error in the development and are therefore only deformed females. To find out the possible effects of these phenotypic males for the whole reproduction complexes, we examined the morphology and the behavior. We could prove that the Poecilia formosa males have a gonopodium, the muscle that moves the gonopodium, a suspensorium and male gonads. With standardized choice experiments we could show that the Poecilia formosa males prefer Poecilia formosa females to Poecilia latipinna females and Poecilia mexicana females. And Poecilia formosa females prefer Poecilia formosa males to Poecilia mexicana males and other Poecilia formosa females. So from the behavior we could expect a normal intraspecific reproduction, as well. On top of these results we got a couple of broods of Poecilia formosa males and Poecilia formosa females since September last year.

22346: Pseudoplatystoma corruscans is a migratory species of economic interest. It is widely distributed in South America (in the basins of the Paraná, San Francisco and Paraguay Rivers) and reproduces in floodplain lagoons where it spends the first phases of its life. Monthly collections, from January 1985 to January 1988, were performed in 150 km of Paraná River, State of São Paulo, Brazil. A total of 255 fish were examined (56% young and 44% adults) measuring between 20.0 and 170.0 cm in total length. Data on body length at first sexual maturation was estimated to be 73.0 cm. This is larger than minimum capture size for this specie determined by the Brazilian Environmental Agency regulating fishing. The reproductive period coincided with the flood period from October to January and schools of mature fish were followed as far as Rio Pardo, a tributary of the Paraná River. In the next months P. corruscans larvae were always collected in marginal ponds. These periodic floods promote the contact of the Paraná River with the marginal ponds and are a requirement to the maintenance of the reproductive processes of P. corruscans.
